# 4. IAM Access Analyzer
# Section: Identity & Federation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/34785522
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's discuss IAM Access Analyzer.
And this is a service within the IAM console
that is used to find out
which resources are going to be shared externally.
So this applies with S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys,
Lambda functions and layers,
SQS queues, and Secrets Manager Secrets.
So the idea is that some of these, obviously,
can have resource policies attached to them,
or they can be shared with other accounts.
But sometimes you forget about sharing these items
and it can be a security risk for your company
because some of the data may be
accessible by external sources.
And so, you define a zone of trust,
which is going to correspond to your AWS accounts
or your entire AWS organization.
And then anything outside your zone of trust
that has access to the resources said above
are going to be reported as findings.
So for example, we have an S3 bucket,
we can share it with a specific role, a user, an account,
an external client by IP, or a VPC endpoint.
But if we define the zone of trust to be our accounts
and only the role, the user, and the VPC endpoints
are within our accounts,
then the accounts and the external clients
are going to be flagged as a finding,
and you can look at it within the console
to take action if you think this is a security risk.
There are other sides of IAM Access Analyzer
you need to know about.
So first of all, you can do policy validation
on IAM Access Analyzer.
So you can validate your policy
against the policy grammar and best practices.
You're going to get general warnings,
security warnings, errors, and suggestions,
as well as actionable recommendations
on how to improve your policies.
But also you can generate policies
directly from IAM Access Analyzer.
And that's really cool
because it's actually going to generate an IAM policy
tailored to your access activity
based on the API calls that have been made.
So let's take an example of a Lambda function
doing API calls into an S3 bucket
or a Kinesis Data Stream.
Then, of course, these API calls
are going to be logged into CloudTrail.
Now, what's going to happen is that
the CloudTrail logs are going to be reviewed
by the IAM Access Analyzer feature to generate a policy
and then is going to get fine-grained permissions
with the appropriate actions and services.
So IAM Access Analyzer review the logs.
And it's up to 90 days of logs.
And then, out of it, will generate an IAM policy
that is going to be most likely security best practice
because it will encompass
all the API calls that your application has been making
over the past 90 days.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

because thanks to this, well,
you have the same key in multiple regions,
and that means that you can encrypt in one region
and decrypt in the other regions using the same KMS key ID.
So you don't need to re-encrypt data
or make cross-region API calls.
So they will have the same key ID, the same key material,
the same automatic rotation, and so on.
But these keys are not global keys, okay?
It's this principle that there is a primary key
in one region, and all the others are replicas.
Each key can be managed independently,
and although you can only have one primary key at a time,
it's possible for you
to promote one replica into their own primary key.
So the use cases for multi-region keys
is going to be disaster recovery, global data management,
for example, for DynamoDB global tables,
active-active application that span multiple region,
or distributing signing applications, and so on.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

by using VPC peering, for example.
CloudHSM has cryptographic acceleration
for SSL and TLS and Oracle TDE.
In terms of access and authorization, KMS is using IAM,
whereas CloudHSM is using their own users
and you have to manage your own permissions
from within the CloudHSM device itself.
For high availability,
well, this is embedded in the KMS service.
But for CloudHSM, you need to have multiple HSM device
over different availability zones.
For audit capability, you have CloudTrail and CloudWatch.
But on top of it,
CloudHSM has multifactor authentication support.
And finally, there's a free tier for KMS
whereas there's no free tier for CloudHSM.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 24. Solution Architecture - SSL on ELB
# Section: Security
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/18376404
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Let's discuss some solution architecture
when using SSL with a Load Balancer.
So we have this classic architecture
where we have an Auto Scaling group,
and maybe an Application Load Balancer
that has an SSL certificate loaded onto it,
thanks to ACM.
So our users are able to access our Load Balancer
using HTTPS, and then our Load Balancer can be set up
to talk to our EC2 instances using HTTP.
That is something very simple, scalable,
it works really well,
it's classic,
but sometimes you may want to set up
SSL directly on your web server EC2 instances.
Here is an example.
We have an NLB and we have an Auto Scaling group
and we just have TCP connection to the NLB
but we've decided
to perform the HTTPS
at the EC2 instance level
for various reasons
but this is the way it happens.
So you need to have an HTTPS connection happening
from your EC2 instances,
and for it to work
you need to retrieve these SSL certificates
onto these EC2 instances
for them to become an HTTPS web server,
and so for this something you can be doing for example,
is using user data scripts at EC2 boot time
to retrieve certificates from the SSM Parameter Store
and then load them onto your EC2 instances,
and obviously to retrieve these SSL certificates
they will need to be proper IAM role set up
for your EC2 instances,
and that would work,
and your EC2 instances
would be able to provide HTTPS back to your users,
and that would work really well,
but performing SSL encryption and decryption can use up
some valuable CPU resources on your EC2 instances.
On top of it,
you have to extract the SSL certificates
out of your SSM Parameter Store
and that may be some what of a risk problem
if someone was able to SSH into your EC2 instances.
So something you can do though,
is using CloudHSM to do SSL offloading.
So we have the same architecture,
the users talk to the NLB
which forwards to TCP traffic to your EC2 instances
which are in fact HTTPS,
and so for to perform the actual SSL encryption,
you can offload it to CloudHSM using SSL acceleration,
and that's supported by a NGINX, Apache Web servers
and IIS for windows server,
and the idea is that
the CloudHSM device in the backend
will be the one performing the SSL acceleration
or offloading for your EC2 instances,
and that will save up some valuable resources
for your EC2 instances.
So that's a very classic solution architecture as well.
Extra level of security
is that the SSL private key
will never leave the HSM device,
and so it's extra secure.
The only way to make this work
is to set up a cryptographic user,
so CU, on the CloudHSM device
and make sure your EC2 instances can use up that user
and work with that user be stored,
or for example you can store the user name and password
on the SSM Parameter Store.
So you're quite,
you can have so many ways of doing this architecture
but using the CloudHSM-SSL Offloading
is one of the most secure
and one of the most handy as well.
So this is probably something new for you,
and I wanted to show it to you.
So that's it for this lecture.
I will see you in the next lecture.

# 25. S3 Security
# Section: Security
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/18287528

Now let's get into S3 security.
And first of all, we're going to look at S3 encryption.
And it's good to know, first of all,
SSE-S3 which allows you to encrypt S3 objects
using keys handled and managed by AWS.
Then we have SSE-KMS,
where you leverage the KMS service
to manage your encryption keys.
Why would you do this?
Well, first of all, any API call that is done
through SSE-KMS will appear as an API call in KMS,
and therefore, your key usage appears in CloudTrail,
which is very helpful for audit purposes.
The second thing is that it's a very good security
in case your bucket is made public,
because even if an bucket is made public,
or an object is made public,
and that object is encrypted with SSE-KMS,
then it can never be read
because a public anonymous user cannot have access
to your KMS key.
Finally, if you do upload objects
with the SSE-KMS encryption scheme,
you need to make sure that you have access
to the IAM permission, kms:GenerateDataKey,
because this is how the data key is being used
to upload that object specifically.
You also have SSE-C.
So, in that example,
we want to manage our own encryption keys,
but we pass them on to Amazon S3,
and the encryption is done server side.
Or, if you prefer to manage your own encryption keys
and also do the encryption client side,
then you use client-side encryption,
and therefore you encrypt
and your decrypt your data client side.
Finally, if you use Glacier,
all the data is going to be by default AES-256 encrypted,
and the key will remain under the control of AWS.
Now, you also have encryption in transit,
and in that case Amazon S3 will expose two endpoints.
You'll have the HTTP endpoint, which is non-encrypted,
and that's not the default one your client use,
and the default one used by your client
is the HTTPS endpoint to guarantee that you have encryption
in flight using SSL or TLS certificates.
So you can use whatever endpoint you want,
but of course HTTPS is recommended,
and it is actually mandatory if you want
to use the SSE-C encryption scheme.
Finally, if you wanted to force your users to use HTTPS,
then you will use a bucket policy,
and you will use the condition
on the aws:SecureTransport condition.
And we're good to go with encryption in flights.
Next, we have events in S3 buckets,
and so there are multiple ones.
The first one is S3 Access Logs,
which will give you detailed records
of all the requests that are made into a buckets,
and it might take hours to deliver
and it might be delivered to another S3 buckets,
and it might be incomplete.
This is from the documentation, this is best effort,
but still a really good access log to get into S3.
S3 Event Notifications now,
which is to retrieve notifications
whenever certain events happen in your buckets.
For example, new objects are being created,
objects are being removed,
objects are being restored,
or there is a replication event happening,
and the destinations of these S3 events
can be SNS, SQS queue and Lambda.
And so, typically, these S3 event notifications are going
to be delivered within seconds,
but it can sometime take a minute or two,
and you will receive a notification for every single object
if you have enabled versioning on your S3 bucket.
But if somehow you haven't enabled versioning,
and in the very rare occasion that you're doing two writes
at the same time on the same object,
then you may receive just one notification and not two,
and that is outlined in the documentation,
but, for the rest, you will receive a notification
for every single object inserted into your S3 buckets.
Now, for Trusted Advisor, check the bucket permissions.
So this will be helpful, for example,
to know if your bucket is being public.
And you have Amazon EventBridge where you need
to enable CloudTrail object-level logging on S3 first
and then the target of Amazon EventBridge
could be Lambda functions, SQS, SNS, etc, etc.
Next, S3 security, how do you secure a bucket?
Well, first you have user-based security
where you have IAM policies,
and by setting up an IAM policy on one of your user,
you allow it to access a specific bucket.
And you have resource-based policy,
which is bucket policies,
so this is bucket-wide rules for the S3 console,
and we've seen that it's very helpful
when we have cross-account access,
because it allows the accounts
who wants to access the S3 buckets not to assume a role

Then we have object ACL finer grain,
and finally bucket access control list,
which is less common,
and the exam probably will not talk to you about the ACLs,
only talk about the S3 bucket policies

Okay, now let's talk about the S3 bucket policies

The first one is SourceIp.
So this allows you to have a condition

And we have a second one called VpcSourceIp,

But there is another option.
It's called Source VPC or Source VPC Endpoint.
And this is when you define a VPC endpoint,

Okay. Then we have CloudFront Origin Identity.

If you wanna see many different S3 bucket policies,
please use this link and have a look,
learn a little bit more,
if these are not very familiar for you.
So now pre-signed URLs, what are those?
You can generate pre-signed URLs using the SDK or the CLI.
And this for downloads or for uploads, they are both valid.
And the idea is that you sign these URLs
with your IAM credentials.
And so whoever has this pre-signed URL
has exact same right that you were given
when you created that pre-signed URL.
It's valid for a default of one hour,

with the expires-in arguments,
and users will inherit the permission of the person

GET is for download and PUT is for upload.

Okay, so now let's talk about VPC Endpoint Gateway for S3.

Now the S3 bucket has a public access
and, therefore, you need to go through an internet gateway

go through the internet gateway and then get access
through the public internet to the S3 bucket.
Now, the S3 bucket can have a bucket policy,
and we can filter, have a condition for the bucket policy
by using AWS:SourceIP, and this must be a public IP
or an elastic IP, which are public by the way.
That's option one.
Option two is we have a instance in a private subnet,
and we want to access the S3 bucket policy.
Now, there's a way where we could have
this private instance go through a net gateway
in this public subnet, go through the internet gateway

So you go shoop like this up and then right,
but there is a better way, right?
Because here you go through the public internet,

Another way to do this is to use a VPC Endpoint Gateway.
And you define this VPC Endpoint Gateway,
and then all the traffic remains on the AWS network.
It stays private.
And now the idea is that you can access your S3 bucket

and if you wanted to use an S3 bucket policy,
you could have two conditions.
The first one is AWS:SourceVpce,

I hope that makes sense

Okay, finally, for S3 security.
So let's talk about Object Locks and Glacier Vault Lock.
So they're very similar.
S3 Object Lock allows you to adopt a WORM,
so write once, read many model,
which is to block an object version deletion
for a specified amount of time.
So you have the certainty that will never, ever,
ever be deleted.
It's the same for Glacier Vault Lock,
where you adopt the same model,

and you need to prove these to auditors,
then it's a great way to show that,
because you've set up a Object Lock or a Glacier Vault Lock,

# 26. S3 Access Points
# Section: Security
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/30990812
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about S3 access points.
So let's take an example
of an S3 bucket that has a lot of data.
We have finance data, we have sales data,
and we have different users
or groups that want to access their data.
We could create a very complicated S3 bucket policy
and make it grow over time.
The more users, the more data you have,
the more unmanageable this may become.
So what is the solution?
Well, we can create what's called S3 access points.
So we can, for example,
create a finance access point that is going
to be connected to the finance data.
How is it connected to the finance data?
Well, we're going to define an access point policy
and this policy looks just like an S3 bucket policy
and is going to grant read write access
to the finance prefix.
Then we can define a sales access point.
And, again, this will be connected to the sales data
thanks to an access point policy,
a different one attached to this access point,
which is going to grant read and write access
to the sales prefix.
As you can see, I now have two policy
and if I want to have an analytics access point,
well, we can create it so that it points to finance
and sales, but in read only access.
So we're going to create our own read only policy
on the analytics access point.
So you can see here we have pushed the security management
from the S3 bucket policy into the access points
and each access point will have its own security.
Therefore, with the proper IAM permissions
then our users can access the finance access points
and connect only to the finance part of our bucket.
The users as well for sales can only access the sales
and the analytics group can access finance
and sales at the same time.
So by using access points, we define different ways
to access our S3 bucket.
And the result of that is that we have
a very simple way to manage security.
We have policies attached to each access point
and also we have a very simple bucket policy on Amazon S3.
Therefore, we can really scale access to our S3 buckets.
So to summarize access points, simplify security managements
for S3 buckets, and each access point will have
its own DNS name.
That's how you connect to the access point.
You can choose it to be connected to the internet
as an origin or a VPC for private traffic.
And then you attach again an access point policy
which is very similar to bucket policy.
And this allows you to manage security at scale.
Regarding the VPC origin of S3 access points,
we can define them to be privately accessible.
So that's, for example, an EC2 instance
in a VPC access says without going through the internet
our S3 bucket through the VPC access point
through a VPC origin.
So to do so, to get access to this VPC origin,
we must create what's called a VPC endpoint
to access the access point.
So it's something in our VPC that will allow us to connect
privately into the access point through our VPC origin.
And then the VPC endpoint has a policy,
and this policy must allow access
to the target buckets and the access points.
So the VPC endpoint policy will allow our EC2 instance
to connect to both the VPC, the access points
on Amazon S3 and the S3 buckets.
So in this case, we have VPC endpoint for security.
We also have security for the access point policy
and security at the S3 bucket level.
All right. That's it for access points.

# 27. S3 Multi-Region Access Points
# Section: Security
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/36230426
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So you also have the possibility
to define multi-region access points on Amazon S3.
The idea is that with this access point,
you have a global endpoint
that will span multiple S3 buckets in multiple regions.
And the idea is that you access it only through one endpoint
and this endpoint will redirect you to the S3 bucket
that makes sense in the region that makes sense.
So it's going to dynamically route requests
to the nearest S3 bucket,
therefore providing you the lowest latency
and to make sure that while the data
in all the S3 buckets are equal,
you have bidirectional replication.
So the data is replicated
from one bucket to the next and vice versa.
This way, all your regions are synchronized
and we'll see as well, we have failover controls,
so it's possible for us to define all buckets are active,
or to have some buckets as a backup, so as a passive,
so that if we failover if there's a region problem,
then we can failover to the passive buckets.
So let's have a look at, for example,
an example with three regions.
We have US-EAST-1, EU-WEST-1, and AP-SOUTHEAST-1,
with the same S3 bucket
that's going to be replicated across all regions.
So automatically, these roles are created
by Amazon S3 for you,
so you just have to say it.
But then all the data within these buckets is
going to be replicated no matter what.
And as you can see, we must have replication rules
across all buckets to one another.
Then we create this S3 multi-region access point.
And then when our application is going to
request an S3 bucket object
then we're going to be routed automatically
to the region with the lowest latency.
And in case this region is down
then we may be redirected into the other regions.
So then we have the fellow rear controls I told you
about for your S3 access point.
So let's take an example of a bucket that's across
that's replicated across two regions.
Okay? And we have a multi-region access point.
Now in the case of an active passive fellow rear control
where you're going to designate one bucket as active
and the other one as passive.
Therefore whenever we request an object.
We're not going to go this time to the lowest latency
we're just going to go to the one that's active.
And of course, if you have multiple active ones
you will have the lowest latency.
And in case you will have a regional traffic discretion
for example, US-East-1 is experiencing a bad outage
then automatically you're going to have a failover initiated
and your request will go to the passive S3 bucket
which no matter what will contain all your data.
And these kind of failover controls are valid
for active/passive type of setups, but also active/active.
This is when you can write to multiple regions at a time.
Alright, that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

So there is another use case for EFS three access points

but you want to modify the object

duplicating our buckets to have different versions
of each object, we can use S3 Object Lambda instead.

in this S3 bucket
and so they're able to access directly the S3 buckets
and put and get the original object out of it.
But then an analytics application may want to
only have access to the redacted object.

what we can do is that we create an S3 access point
on top of a S3 bucket and is connected to a Lambda function.

the analytics application accesses our S3 Object
Lambda access points, which invokes our Lambda function.

from the S3 bucket and runs some code to redact the data.

obtaining a redacted object from the very same S3 bucket

loyalty database to enhance the data.
So instead of, again, creating a new S3 bucket and

Lambda access point on top of it.

this S3 object Lambda access point to get, again

# 30. DDoS and AWS Shield
# Section: Security
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/34785352
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Next, we're getting into DDoS attacks.
So DDoS stands for Distributed Denial of Service.
It's a way to basically shut down an instance
by making it sure it cannot accept any new traffic
effectively making it useless
and so your users cannot access your application anymore.
So the way it works that you have an attacker
and you have the application server,
and the attacker through some various techniques,
that we'll not get into,
will be able to have a bunch of computers
that are going to be masters
and they're going to create bots
and the bots will be a lot of them
and all the bots are going to get into requesting
stuff from our application server in very bad ways,
non-conventional ways,
and so the application server is overwhelmed,
it doesn't know how to respond to this request.
It's going to try as best as it can,
but it's gonna be very soon overwhelmed
and then it will be just done

cannot access your application server

It's very dangerous, but it's very common on the internet.
And so there are different types of attacks
on your infrastructure.
There is DDoS and so it's when your service isn't available
because it's receiving too many requests at a high level.
So there's different ones.
There's SYN Flood, which is a layer four type of attack
when there's too many TCP connection requests happening.
There's UDP Reflection where other servers
can send a big UDP request to our server.
DNS flood attack, where we overwhelm a DNS
so that users cannot query our DNS service
and then can't find our website, which is bad.
Then the Slow Loris attack, where a lot of HTTP connections,
so it's layer seven, are opened and maintained
and our server is trying to maintain all of them.
The threads are being overwhelmed and the server is useless.
Then there's application level attacks
which is more complex, more specific
and you need to understand how the target application works
to make it an application level attack.
And so before it was network based attack,
now it's application level.
And so you have some things such as case bursting strategy
to overload the backend database with a request
to invalidate the cache
or you request too many things
or you send too many big packets.
It just depends on your application
and the kind of security holes
your developers may have introduced
while programming your application.
Okay, so how do we get protected from DDoS

We have CloudFront and Route 53

and with EventBridge you can run some kind of automations.
So what does Amazon Inspector evaluate?
You have to remember, the Inspector is only
for your running EC2 instances, your Container Images

So talking about this feature,

that has a couple or many EC2 instances

Now let's talk about all the processes

The first one is a launch process

increasing the capacity.
The terminate process that removes
an EC2 instance from the group,

The health check, the process that's checks the health

AZ rebalance which is a process that looks at your ASG

and they will check the correct thing,

So let's make an example.

for example, checks a route on your EC2 instance
called slash health server
and the server that says,
yes I'm alive and I'm functioning correctly.
This is a good health check.
A bad health check is where an auto scaling group

So now let's talk about EC2 spot instances

up to 90% compared to on-demands.

Well, you define a max spot price

save your files, and so on.
So spot instances are great for batch jobs, data analysis
or any kind of workload that is resilient to failure,
but you should not use them for critical jobs
or databases while because they can be reclaimed
by AWS very quickly and you can lose them.
So in terms of the spot price, what does it look like?

for a duration of three months in US East 1.

So if you have one A, one B, one C, et cetera,
you have a different price and the price can vary over time.
So if you define your user max price at here,
this dotted black line that's horizontal,
then as long as the price is underneath that black line,
we get an instance,
and then as long as it's above it, we lose, we terminate
or stop that instance.
And so as we can see, the spot price is quite lower
than the on-demand price.
So if your user defined max price, it's very high,
then you will never lose your spot instance
based on this graph.

that we'll make sure that if you lose your spot instance

Okay, next spot fleets.

that's what it's called a fleet.

because, well, Amazon S3 will trigger a notification
in Amazon SNS which will immediately invoke
a Lambda function,
and you can go very high on the concurrency level
if you have a lot of notifications in SNS.
So therefore, for every image in Amazon S3,
Lambda is going to be triggered as fast as possible
and you're going to get a lot of parallel executions.
Now, if some of these do not go well,
you may lose some data.
You need to use a DLQ
to make sure the failed Lambda attempts
do end up somewhere.
Now, if you are using the second architecture,
then the messages go from Amazon S3 into SNS
into an SQS queue.
So this happens as fast as possible
and the SQS queue will fill up.
But then Lambda functions will obviously scale as well,
but they will consume batch of messages
and process them one by one.
And so one Lambda function
will have 10 messages, for example,
and the second one will also have 10.
And so the queue will not empty as fast as possible.
So you're going to get batch execution,
is going to be a bit more efficient,
but there's gonna be a bit of delay
from when the file is uploaded onto Amazon 3
and processed by a Lambda function.
But in case you have Lambda function failures,
well, the messages are going to be kept in Amazon SQS.
Okay, so that's it for the second part of Lambda.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

With the client connecting to the Cognito User Pool,

# 59. Route 53 - Part 1
# Section: Compute & Load Balancing
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/18376466
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk about Route 53.
And first, let's talk about the record types
that exist within Route 53.
So we have the A that maps a hostname to IPv4.
Quadruple A which maps the hostname to IPv6.
We have CNAME to map a hostname to another hostname
in which the target of the hostname
is being A or an AAAA record.
And you cannot create a CNAME on top of,
the top node of the DNS namespace which is the Zone Apex.
So, you cannot create a CNAME for example.com.
We can create a CNAME for www.example.com,
and we'll see how to solve that problem with Alias records.
And then finally, NS
which are name servers for the hosted zone
which control how traffic is rooted to a domain.
So, these records are all you need to know
for the Solutions Architect professional exam,
so, don't worry about the rest.
Now, for the A record, how does that work?
Well, the client wants to access an EC2 instance
that has a public IP,
is going to first query for example.com in Amazon Route 53,
and then get an IP back, and then thanks to the IP,
reach our EC2 instance.
So, this is for a very simple A record, okay?
Now, let's talk about difference of CNAME and Alias.
So, all the resources in AWS,
for example Load Balancer, CloudFront, et cetera,
they expose an AWS hostname.
So, for example, this is the hostname of a Load Balancer,
and maybe we want this Load Balancer
to be instead myapp.mydomain.com.
So, how do we do this?
Well, if we have a CNAME, as remembered,
it is a hostname that points to any other hostnames.
So, it is very possible for us to do app.mydomain.com
points to anything.com,
and so therefore it would work for the example above,
but this only works for non root domain,
so, it must be something.mydomain.com.
So, for an Alias record though it has difference.
It's to point hostname only to a specified AWS resource.
So, it's app.mydomain.com into something.amazonaws.com,
so, it must be a resource from AWS,
and this works for root domain and non root domain.
So, it works for mydomain.com and it's free of charge
and it has native health check as a feature,
so that means that for the Load Balancer in AWS
you cannot do a CNAME for mydomain.com,
but you can do an Alias record for mydomain.com.
In terms of the targets for the Alias records
we get Elastic Load Balancers, CloudFront Distribution,
API Gateway, Elastic Beanstalk environments, S3 websites,
VPC interface endpoints, Global accelerator Accelerator,
as well as any other Route 53 record
in the same hosted zone.
And you cannot set Alias record for an EC2 DNS name.
Now each record in Route 53 is going to have a record TTL
which is the Time To Live.
So here's an example,
the client wants to talk to our web server,
but we have a DNS request for myapp.example.com.
We're going to get a response, for example A record,
but this will have a TTL,
and this response is going to be cached
for the time of the TTL.
And then once the TTL expires
then the record will be renewed.
So while the TTL is still present
and the record is saved on the client side,
then the requests are going to go to the IP
that was refetched from before.
So, in case you do a high TTL, for example, 24 hours
that means that you're going to get less traffic
on the Route 53,
but you have possibly updated records,
for example, if you update them in DNS side
then it will take up to 24 hours
for clients to get the new values.
Otherwise, if you set a very low TTL,
for example 60 seconds
that means you're going to get more traffic on the DNS side
which is going to cost you some money,
but on the flip side,
the records are going to be outdated for less time
and it's going to be easier to change records,
so, it's always a trade off.
And except for the Alias record
the TTL is mandatory for each DNS record,
very important to remember.
Okay, now let's look at the routing policy,
so we have the simple routing policy
which is to route traffic to a single resource
and this cannot be associated with the health check
and this is the only kind of routing policy
that is not associated with the health check.
So, here's an example, so client goes to food.example.com
and then gets a value back. Super simple.
But you can also specify multiple values in the same record,
and if that's the case
then a random one is going to be chosen by the clients.
So the client is asking for a DNS request
and then gets multiple values as a result.
The client is going to choose a random value.
Okay, that's very simple.
Next, we have Weighted.
So, Weighted gives you the ability
to control the percentage of the request
that go to a specific resource.
So in this example,
we have 70% of the request going to my first EC2 instance
then 20% to my second EC2 instance
and then 10% to my last EC2 instance.
So, this kind of record
can be associated with the health checks
to make sure that we don't send traffic
to a resource that is not healthy.
The use cases for Weighted records is around
load balancing between regions,
testing the application versions, and so on.
Then we have latency based records
which is to redirect resources
that have the least latency close to us
which is super helpful when latency is a user priority.
And the latency is going to be defined on the traffic
between the users and the specified AWS region.
So, it's further possible for Germany users
to be directed to the US, if that's the lowest latency,
and for example, your app is in Asia.
So, these kind of records can be associated
with health checks as well
which gives a failover capability.
So if we have, for example, two ALB,
one in US-East-1 and one in AP-Southeast-1,
and our users all around the world
it's very possible for these users to go to US-East-1
and for the others to go to AP-Southeast-1.
Next we have Failover for active-passive type of record.
So, we have a primary record
and then a secondary disaster recovery record.
And so there's going to be a health check performed
on the primary one.
And then in case the primary fails
then we are going to have a failover to the second instance.
And this will be characterized by DNS request
that either reply with the first EC2 instance
or the second EC2 instance.
Then we have Geolocation
which is different from latency based,
so this is to route based on the user location itself.
So you can specify by continent, by country
or even by US states.
And if you have overlapping
then the most precise location is going to be selected.
So you should create a default record
in case you have no match on location.
And then use case for geolocation is to be
doing website localization, to restrict content distribution
or load balancing.
And these can be associated with health checks, so,
here's an example, we have a map of Europe right here,
and some Germany users could be sent to this record,
French users could be sent to that record
and then anyone else could be sent
to the default IP right here.
Another one is called Geoproximity
which is to route to resources
based on the geographic location of users and resources.
And thanks to something called the bias
you can shift traffic to some resources more or less
based on that number.
So, you change the specify, you change the bias value
to expand traffic to resource,
you're going to increase it from one to 99
or to shrink you're going to decrease it
from minus one to minus 99
which is going to send less traffic to the resource.
And the resource can be an AWS resource
or it could be a non-AWS resource,
and in that case, we need to specify
a latitude and longitude for the Geoproximity
and for it to be effective and to be set up,
you need to use the traffic flow feature of Route 53.
So, it's better to see where the diagram, how that works.
So, if you have US-East-1 and US-East-1
then they're going to be bias zero zero,
so you're going to get a line in the center of the US
geographically.
And so half the users are gonna go to West
and half the users are gonna go to East.
But in case you increase the bias in US-East-1
and for example, you set a bias to something much higher,
say 50,
then if you leave it to zero on US-West-1
then the line is going to be closer to US-West-1
and therefore more users to the right of that line
are gonna go to US-East-1,
and the other ones are gonna go still to US-West-1.
So with the bias you're able to really
manipulate how much proximity you want users to be
next to locations.
Which brings onto Traffic flow.
So traffic flow is a feature of Route 53
which allows you to easily create and maintain
very complex and large records
as well as Geoproximity records.
So it's a visual editor and it gives you
complex routing decision trees available to you
that you can set up easily.
And these configurations are saved as Traffic Flow Policies,
and they can even be applied
to different hosted zones if it needs to,
and they support versioning.
Finally, we have one last type of record
called the Multi-Value record
which is to use when routing to multiple resources,
and then the Route 53 is going to return
multiple values and resources.
But because this can be associated with a health check
we can only make sure that the return values
are full healthy resources.
So the Multi-Value returns up to eight healthy records
at each query.
And a Multi-Value is a good balancer,
but it's not a substitute for having a load balancer.
So here's an example,
We can set up a multi A record to set two multiple IPs,
and then if they're all healthy
then they will all be returned back to the clients.
So now let's talk about another routing policy
called the IP-based routing
which is very intuitive to think about
because you're going to define the routing
based on the client IP addresses.
In Route 53, you're going to define a list of CIDRs,
they are IP ranges for your clients.
And you're going to say based on the CIDR
which location the traffic should be sent to.
So the use cases will be to optimize performance
because you know the IP ahead of time
or to reduce network costs
because you know where the IP is are coming from.
So, an example is that if you know
that you have a specific internet provider and they have,
they are using a specific CIDR of IP addresses.
You can route them to a specific endpoint
thanks to this strategy.
So let's go for an example,
in Route 53 I'm going to define two locations
with two different CIDR blocks.
As you can see, one start with 203
and the other one start with 200.
And the defined IP ranges.
Now, we are going to link these locations
to a specific record.
So for example.com, we're going to have location one,
so the first CIDR block to send to the value 1,2,3,4,
and the second location, the block CIDR number two
to send to 5,6,7,8,
and these represents the public IP of two EC2 instances.
Now, as you would expect,
if a user comes in with a specific IP
that is part of the location one CIDR block,
they will be directed to the first EC2 instance
of IP 1,2,3,4.
And the user B with a second IP address
that belongs to the location two,
will be redirected and will have a DNS query response
to the EC2 instance of IP 5,6,7,8.
So that's it for the basics of Route 53,
I hope there is nothing new for you,

Onto Health Checks, so you get Public

# 61. Route 53 - Resolvers & Hybrid DNS
# Section: Compute & Load Balancing
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/30991252
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's view an advanced use case
that comes up a lot in the exam, which is around Hybrid DNS.
So we have our region and there is the Route 53 resolver.
And by default, this resolver is going
to automatically answer DNS queries
for local domain names for EC2 instances.
So for example, here's our VPC.
We have an EC2 instance.
There is this DNS name,
the Route 53 resolver knows how to reply to these queries.
So this is fine.
Any records in your private hosted zone as well
is going to be easy to answer to,
and records in public name servers,
for example, for a public hosted zone,
or any name server out there that is public on the internet.
Now, if you want to resolve DNS queries
between your VPC and other private networks,
your own networks that has other DNS resolvers,
then you're going to need a hybrid DNS.
So these networks can be PeeredVPC for example,
or it could be an on-premises network that is going
to be connected to our VPC
through Direct Connect or AWS VPN.
So for this, let me introduce you two concepts
that we're going to see with diagrams in the next slides.
So these are about resolver endpoints.
So there is two things.
There's an inbound endpoint and an outbound endpoint.
So inbound endpoints are allowing DNS resolvers
on your external networks to forward DNS queries
to your Route 53 resolver and answer these queries.
So these resolvers will help to resolve domain names
for the resources of AWS.
For example, your EC2 instances or records
that you create in your Route 53 private hosted zone.
So you get both answers for your internal systems,
and also for AWS private host zones,
and I will show you a diagram,
it will make a lot more sense very, very soon.
Now, your outbound endpoint is
to conditionally forward DNS queries
to your on-premises DNS resolvers.
And for this, we're going to create resolver rules
to forward them.
Now we associate these endpoints with one or more VPCs
within the same region,
and we create in two availability zones
for high availability.
Now each endpoint supports
about 10,000 queries per second, per IP address.
And if you need more, well, you create more IP addresses.
And these resolvers remove the need from before
where people have to run their own DNS resolvers
on AWS and link them to their resolvers on premises.

# 62. AWS Global Accelerator
# Section: Compute & Load Balancing
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/30990950
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about AWS Global Accelerator.
This is a way for you to leverage the internal network
of AWS to route to your application.
And for this, it will use what's called an Anycast IP,
and two of them will be created for your application.
Now the Anycast IP is going to be used
to send traffic directly to the Edge locations
all around the world.
And then from the Edge location, the traffic will be sent
to your application, but using the internal traffic of AWS.
How does that work?
Well say that all your applications wants to access
a public ALB in India,
but your clients are in Australia, America, and Europe,
well, the way it's going to work is that they're going
to use the Anycast IP, which is going to redirect them
to an Edge location.
And from the Edge location,
the traffic will go privately on the Edge OS network
from the Edge location into your desired endpoints.
This global accelerator really gives you
some of course, accelerations.
The targets can be Elastic IPs, EC2 instances,
ALB, NLB, could be public or private.
It supports IP preservation of your clients,
except for the Elastic IP endpoints.
You're going to get consistent performance
because, well, you're going to get intelligent routing
from the lowest latency,
and you're also going to get fast regional failover.
You're going to get no issue with client cache,
because the IP does not change.
So your two Anycast IP are going to be there
for the rest of your lifecycle of Global Accelerator,
and it will leverage the internal AWS network
as fast as possible.
In terms of health checks,
while the Global Accelerator performs health checks
of your application, which makes your application global.
And in case something is unhealthy,
then the failover happens usually in less than one minutes.
It's great for disaster recovery then,
because of the health checks with a fast recovery time.
For security, only two external Anycast IP
need to be whitelisted, which is great.
And you're going to get DDoS protection
thanks to AWS Shield.
So what's the difference between CloudFront
and Global Accelerator?
Well, they both use the global network of AWS,
and they both leverage the Edge locations around the world.
They all have integration with SHIELD for DDoS protection,
but CloudFront is here by giving you cached content
at the Edge, such as images or videos,
or dynamic content such as API acceleration
and dynamic site delivery.
But for CloudFront, all the content is going
to be delivered at the Edge, whereas Global Accelerator
is here to improve performance overall.
And it could be not only for HTP but also for TCP or UDP.
And it's going to proxy packets directly
from an Edge location into your application running,
wherever it's running in the AWS network.
And therefore it's going to be a good fit
for non-HTTP use cases such as gaming
for UDP, IOT using MQTT, or Voice over IP.
And it's also going to be great if you have an HTTP use case
that requires to use a static IP address,
or if you have a use case that requires deterministic
fast regional failover.
Okay, that's it.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

So now let's talk about EFS,

that are going to live within the same region
but in different availability zones,
so that's why it's called a network file system.
And it's also going to work for your on-premises servers
if you mount them,
and first, you need to connect your on-premise environment,
of course to AWS, using direct connect or VPN connection.
It's highly available, it's scalable.
It's quite expensive.
It's about three times the cost of gp2,
and you're going to pay per gigabyte use,
which I think is quite a cool model,
whereas for EBS, you have to pay per gigabytes provisions.
So your EFS file system will be living on AWS,
and you'll have a security group attached to it.
And your EC2 instances, for example,
across three different AZs,
if you set up the security groups correctly,
can mount and access your EFS file system.
So if we look at it, the use cases for EFS
are going to be content management,
web data serving, data sharing.
WordPress is a really good candidate.
And for it to work, you need to have a Linux-based AMI.
So Windows does not work with EFS.
It's very important to understand this
from an exam perspective.
And overall, the file system that you're going to use
must be POSIX-compliant,
which is a good use case for Linux.
It uses the NFSv4.1 protocol.
And to control access to EFS, you must use security groups.
You get encryption arrest using KMS,
and you can only attach it into one VPC,
and you create one mount target,
one elastic network interface, ENI, per AZ.
So as I said, it's POSIX file system, so that means Linux,
and it has a standard file API.
The file system will scale automatically,
which I think is really, really nice.
So you can scale from one gigabyte to terabytes, of course.
You pay per usage,
so you only pay for the number of gigabytes you have
in your file system.
So there is no capacity planning
happening behind the scenes.
Now, the very important part about EFS
is to understand the performance and storage classes.
Then we have different performance and storage classes.
So the first, the scale about EFS,
you get thousands of concurrent NFS clients
and 10 gigabytes plus of throughputs,
and you can grow to a Petabyte-scale network file system
automatically, which is really nice.

at the EFS network file system creation time,
and you have several options.
The first one is General Purpose, which is a default.

such as a web server, a CMS, et cetera.
But if you wanted to maximize throughput, you have Max I/O,
which is a higher latency kind of network file system,
but higher throughput, and it's highly parallel.
So it's great if you have big data applications
or media processing needs.
Now, throughput mode, you have different options.
The first one is Bursting.
So you have one terabyte,
means that it's 50 megabytes per second
plus burst up to 100 megabytes per second.
So that's the kind of bursting you get.
You don't have to remember the numbers,
but just to give you an idea.
Provisioned is when you want to set your throughput
regardless of your storage size.

as we have more storage,
but with Provisioned, you can have one gigabyte per second
for one terabyte of storage,
that is fine because you have de correlated
your throughput from your storage.
And finally, to make things a little bit simpler,
you have Elastic,
to automatically scale the throughput up and down
based on your workload.
So, for example,
you can get up to 3 gigabytes per second for reads,

Now for storage classes, we have several options.

# 72. S3 Solution Architecture
# Section: Storage
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/18376512
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay so, finally let's get
into some solution architecture around Amazon S3.
So a common question is how do you expose static objects
to your clients?
A option that's very simple would be
to have an EC2 instance that's going
to be publicly accessible, and maybe you'll have
an EBS volume or maybe it'll be an instance store,
and the data will be stored on it.
It's cheap, it works, it doesn't scale very well
it's not very highly available, but it works,
it's one way of doing things,
a more scalable way, what's a more global way,
would be to have CloudFront in front of this.
So CloudFront talks to EC2, talks to EBS,
and CloudFront gives us a really good benefit
is that now our data is going to be cached
across the global edge network of AWS,
which gives us clients to all around the world,
some ability to get the objects
maybe a little bit closer to them.
So this has a better global availability,
still in the back end, it's not perfect
because in case our EC2 instance fails
then CloudFront will report it that it's unavailable
if it's not cached in its edge network.
So it's an improvement, but not perfect.
Then we can go to a full blown solution
where we have cloud fronds in front
of an application load balancer,
that has a fleet of EC2 instances
behind another scaling group.
And then these EC2 instances need to share some data,
they need to have the same access to the same files
so EBS does not work in this file.
In this use case, sorry.
And then we have to use something like EFS
as a network file system.
The cool thing about EFS, that's an network file system,
it's POSIX compliant,
it does only works for Linux, so it scales.
So this works but this is quite expensive, I would say,
and I would say the last kind of solution
that you would run into
would be CloudFront directly in front of S3.
And this works great.
If you have static objects in S3 that are pretty big.
And that doesn't require them to be updated very often.
So as you can see there's different ways
of exposing static objects, and there's not right way
of doing it, obviously I think the preferred way
is going to be the one with CloudFront and S3.
But still, depends on your architecture, your requirements,
and the way your application
is going to be designed.
Moving on with S3,
as I said, there is no indexing facility in S3
so you cannot search your S3 buckets for an object.
And so the right way of doing things
would be to index objects in DynamoDB.
So you have rights into Amazon S3,
and then maybe through some S3 event notifications,
your Lambda function is being triggered,
it will read part of the file row, the entire file,
but most likely part of the file using a byte range fetch,
and then it will insert some metadata,
some information about your file into DynamoDB table.
And it's really good to have DynamoDB table
because from there, we could create an API
to search for object metadata.
For example, if you have the right index you can search
by date, you can look at the total search used
by a customer, you can list all the objects
with an attribute, and you can find all the objects uploaded
within a date range.
So having the data in DynamoDB
opens up a lot more solutions to search into Amazon S3
and they're a very very good combo, usually linked
with a Lambda function.
So finally some of the best practice we have on Amazon
is to separate the dynamic content from the static content.
I think this makes a lot of sense
but it's good to outline incorrectly.
So if you make a DNS request to Route 53,
you can be redirected for the dynamic content
to for example, your REST API your HTTP server.
So this could be an ALB bus EC2, API gateway plus Lambda.
It really depends.
We've seen this at length already in this course.
But the idea is that you get all the dynamic content
through this route, there's little to no caching, maybe,
and you get access to some fresh, small data.
So you can have the database layer to be DynamoDB,
you can have a caching or session layer index in DynamoDB.
This is just one architecture with the idea I want you
to remember is that it's going to be a more dynamic route
where there's going to be tons of requests,
and for the static content, things
that doesn't change very often, then usually you
go through a CDN layer, such as CloudFront
to cache a content at the edge and save some costs
and improve the performance, there's going to be more
for your HTML files your big files your videos and so on.
And all the static content needs to be stored
onto a layer that scales really well, such as Amazon S3.
It's very possible that your dynamic content has to interact
with Amazon S3 by uploading some files directly in it,
it's possible, definitely.
And then as I said, we can react to changes happening
in our Amazon S3 bucket, using a Lambda function
that reacts to these events,
and the Lambda function could index,
all the data into DynamoDB,
which could in turn help the dynamic route.
So that means that, you know,
even it's though static and dynamic,
they can be definitely linked to one another.
Finally, we don't have to go through CloudFront
to get access to our S3 bucket,
unless we set up an OAI.
But if we haven't, then we can use a pre signed URL
to access our S3 buckets
and get the content right away from it.
And we've seen this when we were trying
to upload files efficiently,
directly into our S3 bucket when we were trying
to download files as well,
in a more performant fashion,

You can never decrease it.

So your FSx for Lustre right now, the clients ask

But the idea is that as soon as you have an S3 bucket
you can just launch Amazon FSx
for Lustre on top of it and start using it.

is going to be loaded only once.

# 83. Lambda@Edge Reduce Latency
# Section: Caching
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/35038504
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So here is a use case for Lambda@Edge
where you can use it to root to a different origin
and reduce the latency of some calls from CloudFront Edge.
So how does that work?
Well say we are using the classic architecture
of an S3 bucket
and then we'll have a CloudFront Edge location.
So it turns out that's if we link these two together,
then it's going to work.
But in case the edge location is far away from the bucket,
then the first request to get some files
may take a long time.
So how do we solve for this?
Well, in the case, for example,
where the users are in Europe
and they want to access our Edge location
if the content is already cashed, then it's perfect.
The object is returned with very, very little latency.
So this is how the edge location works.
But to get the object into the cache,
because the CloudFront edge location is to make a request
from Europe into the US East 1 region
it can have some latency added
which may not be acceptable to you.
So how do we solve for this?
Well, we're going to create a second S3 Bucket,
this time in EU West 2,
and we're going to set up
S3 cross region replication across my two buckets.
The reason we do so is that all the buckets,
all the content of bucket one is now in bucket two
in a region close earth to the user.
Next we're going to create a Lambda@Edge function
which is going to be triggered
by your CloudFront's Edge locations.
And what's going to happen here is that
whenever the users are accessing
the CloudFront Edge location,
the Lambda at edge function is going to look
where the request is coming from.
And if it comes from a region
that is closer to the first bucket
then it's going to direct users to the first bucket.
But else, if the request comes
from a region closer to the second bucket,
then it's going to modify the origin request
and send it to my second origin.
The reason is that the data is the same across both regions,
and so therefore,
the Lambda@Edge function will help us route the request
to the bucket that is the closest to the edge location
thus reducing the latency
of our first call to get a file into an edge location.
Then of course, the object will be returned
and will be good to go.

but a very useful one to reduce the latency

into the CloudFront Edge location
based on Lambda@Edge and different origins.

who want to directly access DynamoDB,
then the right answer is to use DAX.
Because you will scan,
you will have the individual objects
being cached in DAX directly,
and even the results of your query
and your scan will be in DAX.
But let's assume that your client,
after retrieving a lot of the data,
performs some heavy computation.
And this computation can take, I don't know,
10 seconds, 30 seconds.
It can take a long time.
Then you will want to be able to cache the results
of these computations somewhere.
And that's somewhere may be ElastiCache.
So for example, ElastiCache index example could be a place
where you want to store your aggregation results
and make sure other clients can look into ElastiCache
before getting data from DynamoDB
to get the aggregation results.
So it is one kind of architecture.
You could also swap ElastiCache for DynamoDB itself
and have a table act as a cache, it is possible.
But I want to show you here that DAX and ElastiCache
can serve very different purposes, okay?
DAX is going to be for individual object cache
and for query and scan caches in DynamoDB,
whereas ElastiCache is for whatever you wanna put in it.
So it's very possible for you
to perform some heavy computations
and cache them centrally in the ElastiCache
to avoid going back to DAX and DynamoDB
and do some expensive computations again.

Okay, so a quick lecture on SQS.

You don't need to provision anything.
The main purpose to SQS is to decouple between your services

and perform some work asynchronously.
SQS does not handle big messages.
The max message size is 1,024 kilobytes.
So in case you want to send
maybe a 10-megabyte file through SQS,
you would instead upload that file into Amazon S3
and then retrieve the S3 key for your object
and send that through SQS instead.

by an Auto Scaling group,
or it could be an AWS Lambda function using an event mapper.
Another common architecture with SQS is to use it
as a write buffer for DynamoDB.

you would first write to SQS,
and it could scale seamlessly, so you're fine.
And then you would have an application dedicated
to take these writes from SQS

Finally, there's SQS FIFO for First In and First Out.
It means that the messages are received
and read in the order they were sent.
And then because there is
this ordering constraint with FIFO,
then you get 300 messages per second without batching
or up to 3,000 messages per second with batching,
so there is limited scale here.
Now let's talk about dead-letter queues in SQS.
The idea is that let's get into the scenario
where a consumer fails to process a message
within the Visibility Timeout period.
Then we know that the message
automatically goes back into the queue.
So the consumer reads the message.
Maybe there's a failure.
Maybe we don't have enough time.
The message goes back into the queue.
Now if that thing happens very often,
that can be a problem.
For example, we read again the message,
maybe there's something wrong with the message.
Maybe a consumer doesn't understand the message
or can't process the message.
Then the message will go back into the queue,
and it will happen again.
We'll read the message again from SQS,
and it will go again back into the queue.
So we can set a threshold to how many times this can happen.
And this failure loop can be a big problem,
but we can set a MaximumReceives threshold.
And if that threshold is exceeded,
then we can tell SQS to say,
"Well, this message looks a bit odd.
It looks like it's being processed too many times
and not successfully.
Therefore, send this into a dead-letter queue."
And the dead-letter queue will contain that message
for later processing,
and so the message will be removed from the first queue
and sent into the second one.
Why do we have dead-letter queues?
Well, dead-letter queues are very useful for debugging,
and in case a message goes in a dead-letter queue,
because it is an SQS, you have to process it,
but at least it gives you time
to understand what is happening.
A few things to notice
that the dead-letter queue of FIFO queue
must also be a FIFO queue,
and the dead-letter queue of the Standard queue
must also be a Standard queue.
Finally, because we have a dead-letter queue,
you need to make sure that the messages are processed
before they expire from the queue.
So it's a good idea to set a long time,
for example, 14 days of retention,
from within the dead-letter queue.
And the next feature
for management of your dead-letter queues

in the dead-letter queue
to understand what is wrong with them.

You know they haven't been processed
in the source queue,
and therefore, they are in the dead-letter queue,
and you're going to do a manual inspection

And then you're going to fix your consumer code,
understand why the message wasn't processed
in case the message was correct,
and then what you can do is redrive
that message from the dead-letter queue
into the source SQS queue.
And what's going to happen with this
is that the consumer can now reprocess that message
without even knowing
that the message went into the dead-letter queue,

In terms of idempotency,

you need to make sure that your consumers are idempotent.

That means that if you process the same message twice,
if you do the same action twice,
then the effect will not be duplicated.

# 95. Amazon SNS - SQS Fan Out Pattern
# Section: Service Communication
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/31738494
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about
the SNS plus SQS fan-out pattern.
The idea is that you want a message
to be sent to multiple SQS queues,
but if you send them individually to every SQS queue,
there can be problems associated with it.
For example, if your application crashes in between,
if there are delivery failures,
or if you add more SQS queues down the road.
Therefore we want to use the fan-out pattern.
The idea is that you're going to push once an SNS topic
and then you're going to subscribe as many SQS queues
as you want to the SNS topic.
These queues are subscribers
and they will all receive the messages sent into SNS.
So for example, we have a buying service
that wants to send messages to two SQS queues.
What it will do instead,
it will send one message into an SNS topic,
and the queues are subscribers of that SNS topic
so that the fraud service and the shipping service
can read all messages from their own SQS queues.
The idea with this as well
is that it's a fully decoupled model
and there is no data loss.
SQS will give you data persistence, delayed processing,
as well as retries of work.
And with this pattern, we can add more SQS queues
as a subscriber of the SNS topic over time.
For this, we need to make sure
that your SQS queue access policy,
as we've seen from before,
allows your SNS topic to write to your SQS queue.
So again, yet another use case
for using queue access policies,
and we have cross-region delivery.
So it's definitely possible for an SNS topic
in one region to send messages
to SQS queues in other regions if the security allows it.

For example, S3 events into multiple queues.
So there is a limitation of S3 event rules
is that for a combination of event type, for example,
an object is being created
and a prefix, for example,
images/, you can only have one S3 event rule.

to multiple SQS queues?

and we will subscribe many SQS queues
to the SNS topic as a final pattern.

And then what we get from this is that the message

is going to go to many different destinations

Another architecture is that you can send data

So the idea is that with SNS FIFO,
we get the same features as SQS FIFO,
we get ordering by message group ID.
We get deduplication using a deduplication ID
or content-based deduplication.
And both SQS standard and FIFO queues can be subscribers.
In terms of throughput, you're limited.
You get the same throughput as the SQS FIFO queue.
So why do we need this?
Well, in case you wanna do a fan out using SQS FIFO.
So you need fan out, ordering and deduplication.
So the buying service will send the data
into an SNS FIFO topic,
and then it will fan out to two SQS FIFO queue,
which can have the fraud service
and the shipping service read from FIFO queues as well.
One last feature of SNS that can be really handy
regarding the fan-out pattern
is that you can do message filtering in SNS.
So what is message filtering?
Well, it's a JSON policy that is used
to filter messages sent to the SNS topics subscription.
So if a subscription doesn't have a filter policy,
it will receive every message,
and that's a default behavior.
But let's take an example of what happens
when we set up a message filtering policy.
So we have a buying service
and it sends transactions into an SNS topic.
For example, the transaction looked like
there's an order number,
there's a product, for example, a pencil,
the quantity for, and the state which is placed.
Now we want to create an SQS queue just for placed orders,
not all the orders, but just for placed orders.
So for this, we will subscribe the SQS queue
into the SNS topic, and we'll apply a filter policy in JSON,
and we will specify in a policy
that we want to have State equals Placed.
And so only the messages matching the policy
will go into the SQS queue,
but then we could have an SQS queue for canceled orders.
And so we can create our own filter policy for canceled
orders and have those coming from the same SNS topic
into the SQS queue.
And so the placed orders
and the canceled orders SQS queue
will not have the same messages.
We can also use the same filter policy, the canceled one,
to create an email subscription for canceled orders.
We could have a filter policy for declined orders,
for example, and as another SQS queue,
or we can create an SQS queue without a filter policy
to have all messages from that SNS topic.
So using all these fan-out patterns and message filtering,
FIFO queues and FIFO topics,
we get lots of different possibilities
and the exam will try to test you on all of those.
So that's it for this lecture.

# 96. Amazon SNS - Message Delivery Retries
# Section: Service Communication
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/34783322
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, let's do a deep dive
on the Message Delivery Retries
and SNS dead letter queues.
So, when a message is delivered to an SNS subscriber,
in case you have service side errors,
a delivery policy is applied.
So, it means if the endpoint that SNS
is calling is having issues.
And this is a table that makes it look
like what is going to happen.
So, if you look at the AWS manage endpoint, for example,
can you firehose, lambda or SQS?
Immediately, there's gonna be three times
without delay or retry.
So that's maybe the message will go through.
If it doesn't go, then it goes
into a pre backup phase
where it's tried two times one second apart.
Then it goes into a backup phase where it's tried 10 times
with exponential backup from one second to 20 seconds.
And then, if it doesn't work still,
it goes into the past backup phase
where it's tried 100,000 times 20 seconds apart.
So the total attempts is over 100,015 times
over the course of 23 days.
So as you can see, there is a lot of retries
for the manage endpoints of AWS.
And there's another one for SMTP.
But the idea here is that there is a delivery policy
and retries are being made
until a success happens, hopefully.
In case you have an HTP endpoint
that you set up as a subscriber to your SNS topic.
Then you have support for custom policies.
So, you may want to say
what is the number of retry, the min delay, the max delay
the backoff function, the throttle policy, and so on
to really customize how SNS will retry for your backend
because your backend may not like heavy load
or a heavy number of retries.
So this is the only kind of delivery mechanism
that supports a custom delivery policy.
That's very important for you to remember.
Next, we have Dead Letter Queues.
So, in case you have exhausted the delivery policy,
then the messages that haven't been delivered
are going to be discarded,
unless we set a Dead Letter Queue.
And the DLQ is dissimilar to what we have for SQS.
So, DLQ are again, SQSQ queues or SQS FIFO queues,
in case you use SNS FIFO.
And they're attached to a subscription, not to a topic.
So, let me make it clear.
The SNS topic receives messages
and we have two subscriptions.
We have an email subscription and an HTTP subscription
and we can see how these could have issues.
For example, if my email server has issues,
then you may have a problem
or if your HTTP subscription has issue,
again you can have problems.
So, you can set up a Dead Letter Queue
for your email subscription
and you can set up another Dead Letter Queue
for your HTTP subscription.
This guaranteeing that you can process these messages
that were not successful, in case that happens.

Another analytics service you will see
is Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka,
also called Amazon MSK.
And what is Kafka?
Well, Kafka is an alternative to Amazon Kinesis.
Kafka and Kinesis both allow you to stream data.
So, MSK is the ability to get
a fully-managed Kafka cluster on AWS.
And it allows you to create, update
and delete clusters on the fly.
And MSK is going to create and manage Kafka broker nodes
and Zookeeper broker nodes in your cluster for you
and you deploy the cluster in your VPC, across multiple AZ,
up to three for high availability.
You also have automatic recovery from common Kafka failures
and the data is stored on EBS volumes
for as long as you want.
So, from personal experience,
I know it's very difficult to set up Apache Kafka
and the fact you can just do one click
and then deploy Kafka on AWS is great
and this is the Amazon MSK service.
So on top of it, you have the option to use MSK Serverless.
And this is that you run Apache Kafka on MSK,
but this time you don't provision servers,
you don't manage capacity,
automatically MSK will provision resources
and scale, compute and storage for you.
So what is Apache Kafka then?
Apache Kafka is a way for you to stream data
and a Kafka cluster is made of multiple brokers
and then you will have producers that will produce data
and so they will have to ingest data from places,
such as Kinesis, IoT RDS, et cetera, et cetera,
and they will send the data directly
into a Kafka topic that is going to be fully replicated
into other brokers.
Now, this Kafka topic is having real-time streaming
of data and consumers will pull from the topic
to consume the data itself
and then your consumer can do whatever he wants,
process it or send it to various destinations,
such as EMR, S3, SageMaker, Kinesis and RDS.
So the idea is that Kafka is quite similar to Kinesis,
but there are differences to look out for.
So what are the differences between Kinesis Data Streams
and Amazon MSK?
Well, in Kinesis Data Streams,
you have one megabyte message limit,
which is the default in Amazon MSK,
but you can configure it for a higher message retention.
For example, 10 megabytes.
You can have Data Streams with Shards
in Kinesis Data Streams or in MSK,
it's called Kafka Topics with Partitions,
but the concept are sort of similar.
To scale Kinesis Data Stream,
you need to do Shard Splitting and to scale it down Merging.
But in Amazon MSK to scale a topic,
you can only add partitions.
You cannot remove partitions.
You have in-flight encryption for Kinesis data streams
and then you have either plain text
or TLS in-flight encryption for MSK.
You get at-risk encryption for both of these clusters
and, in the exam level, this is enough.
Just so you know, a few differences.
And also for Amazon MSK, you can keep data
for as long as you want, you can go over one year,
as long as you pay for the underlying EBS storage,
you're good to go.
So to produce to MSK you need to create a Kafka Producer
and then to consume from MSK, you have multiple options.
The first one is to use Kinesis Data Analytics
for Apache Flink.
So you want a Flink Application
and you make it read it directly from the MSK cluster.
You can use Glue as well to do streaming ETL jobs

You can use Lambda functions to directly have Amazon MSK

and you can make it run on whatever platform you want,

or an ECS cluster or an EKS cluster.

so they give you a lot of scale to process data.
But then as soon as you're done,
you're more than welcome to shut down your EMR cluster
and that saves you a lot of cost as well.
So EMR is a natural fit
to migrate your Hadoop clusters from on-premise onto AWS.
EMR is going to be launched in the Big Data ecosystem.
So it's going to be made of Apache Spark,
HBase, Presto, Flink, Hive, et cetera, et cetera.
The idea is that usually
Hadoop clusters are quite complicated
to create and configure,
but with EMR, all the provisioning and the configuration
of the EC2 instances is done for you.
You just specify what you want and you get it very quickly.
You also get auto-scaling capability with CloudWatch,
and the use cases for EMR very classically
is data processing, machine learning,
web indexing, big data,
basically anything you need to process at scale.
Now, EMR has a few integrations you need to remember
going into the exam.

and it is within a single availability zone.

and they have EBS volumes
and you can have many of that.
And the EBS volumes are running something called HDFS
for Hadoop Distributed File System,
and that gives you temporary storage
for your EC2 instances in your cluster.
But if you want to have long-term retention of data,
you need to use something called EMRFS,
which has a native integration into S3,
and S3 obviously is going to be
a more durable type of storage because it is multi-AZ,
and that gives you permanent storage
and you can also define server-side encryption.
So as we can see, any EBS volume is going to be
high performance for temporary storage
and for your computations,
but as soon as you need to persist your data
into something that's going to be multi-AZ,
use EMRFS and S3.
As you can see, everything is launched in your EMR cluster
within a single-AZ because you get natural,
better networking performance and lower cost.

in case you lose your AZ
you would lose your data.

and there is a module that has been developed for Hive

you can do it so from EMR by using Hive.
Okay, next, very important, you need to understand
how you can optimize your cost in EMR.
So Amazon EMR is made of clusters of EC2 instances
and you have different kind of nodes.
You have the master node,
and the master node manages the cluster.
It will coordinate and manage the health

Then you have the core node.

And then you have this task node,

predictable type of workloads
and they will never be terminated.
If you use reserved instances,

your reserved instances if possible.

are going to be the master node

and also the core nodes.

well because they can be terminated,
they're less reliable but they're cheaper.

called Redshift Workload Management, WLM.
So it enables you to flexibly manage queries priorities
within workloads.
And the use case for this
is to prevent short fast running queries from getting stuck
behind long running queries.
You can define multiple query queues.
You can define, for example, a super user queue,
user defined queues, and so on.
And then you route your query
to the appropriate queue at runtime.
So in this example, I have Amazon Redshift
and I have three queues.
I have the super user queue, the short running queue,
and the long running queue.
The names are pretty explicit
and say we have two kinds of users.
We have our admin and our user.
So the admin, they want their queries to be done
as soon as possible.
So they will do system queries,
and then these queries will go directly
into the super user queue.
And this will have priority,
the user may have some short running queries,
and these we want to have
into the short running query queue.
This way we are sure that it will just be a lot
of short running queries,
but if the user is submitting a longer running query
and we know it's gonna take a lot of time,
then we should send it directly into the long running queue
to make sure not to block the short running queries.
So we have two kind of workload management.
The first one is automatic WLM,
where the queues and resources are managed by Redshift.
And the second one is manual WLM, where the queues
and resources are managed by you, the user.
Then we have Redshift concurrency scaling.
So this enables you to provide consistently fast performance
with virtually unlimited number of users
and queries by adding Redshift capacity on the fly.
So this additional cluster capacity
is called concurrency scaling cluster and allows you
to process an increase in requests.
So let's say we have a normal Redshift cluster
with a few nodes another,
and then this sustains a bunch of users
that we have normally,
but say tomorrow we get a lot more users submitting queries
into Amazon Redshift,
then automatically the concurrency scaling cluster
will add nodes automatically to accommodate
for this number of users.
Now we get the ability to decide which queries get sent
to the concurrency scaling cluster
using the WLM feature we just saw before.
And this feature is charge per second.
So that's all you need to know about Redshift.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

you need to use a type of data
where you're going to scan less data.

for cost-savings,
because you only scan the columns you need.
So therefore, the recommended formats for Amazon Athena,
are going to be Apache Parquet and ORC,
and it's going to give you a huge performance improvement.

Next, if you know you're going to query all the time

you can partition your datasets,

and each slash will be a different column name

And so you're organizing,
you're partitioning your data in Amazon S3,
so that when you query it,
you can know exactly in which folder
at which path Amazon S3,
you need to scan for data.
So here's an example of data partitions.
