and then we do /year=1991.
So we partition by year,
and we'll have one folder for each year.
Then within each year we'll have month,
so month equals one,
and within each month we'll have days,
this equals one.
And so when I do a query on Athena,
and I filter for a specific year,
a specific month, and a specific day,
then we'll know exactly
to which folder in Amazon S3
to get the data from,
and therefore we'll only recover a subset of the data.
Therefore, we'll have really, really good partitioning.
Finally, the last performance improvement you need to do,

Okay, so now let's talk about
cost savings in S3.
And for this, we'll get started with S3 storage classes.
Now, in the next lecture,
I've included a full lecture detailing exactly
what each storage class does, in case you don't know,
but in case you know, I wanna make this lecture very short
for you in order not to bore you.
So, the first class is S3 Standard-General Purpose.
Then we have S3 Standard-Infrequent Access.
This is when our objects are going
to be infrequently accessed,
and so we want to have some cost saving
by having them being cheaper,
but we're going to pay a little bit more every time
we're trying to access these objects.
Then we're getting S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access.
This is where objects are gonna be cheaper as well
to store in S3, but this time if you lose a full AZ,
then you will lose access to your objects.
So you need to make sure that these objects are recoverable
or can be recreated.
For example, thumbnails from S3 images can be a very good
use case for One Zone IA.
Intelligent Tiering, which is going to be smart enough
to move objects in between the tiers in order to give you
the maximum amount of cost saving.
And you have to pay for that monitoring.
So you have to pay for each object that is being monitored.
But all in all together, you have less management
on your part and you should save some money.
Then we have Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval,
which is a Glacier tier, which allows you
to retrieve your files very, very quickly.
We have Flexible Retrieval where you have more flexibility
into how you want to retrieve your file.
And then Deep Archive for files are going
to be giving you the most cost saving,
but that will take a long time to be retrieved
and to move between all these storage classes,
you can use either manual actions
or you can define an S3 Lifecycle configuration
that will automatically transition your objects
to a different tier after a certain amount of time.
So the first cost saving is going to be using
S3 Lifecycle Rules.
Then we can automatically transition objects between tiers
or even delete objects,
and that will obviously save us some money.
In terms of object storage, if we're able to compress
our objects before sending it into S3,
then we're obviously going to save in storage space
and therefore we'll pay less money.
Finally, there's a feature I haven't mentioned yet,
but it is good to mention it right now,
which is S3 Requester Pays.
With Requester Pays, you're making sure that the person
requesting for the object is going to have to pay
and not you.
So in general, bucket owners pay for all Amazon S3 storage,
their storage, and data transfer costs
associated with their buckets.
But when you enable Requester Pays,
only the requester will pay for the cost of the request
and the data download from the bucket.
So you still have the cost of storing the data
in your bucket, but all the transfer cost to download
the data from the bucket is going to be
at the charge of the requester.
So if you have an object that's, for example,
a large data set, and you need to share it
with like thousands of accounts,
and obviously, you don't want to bear all the network costs
for this, you can enable S3 Requester Pays,
and then each account that will request the data
from your bucket will have to pay the data transfer
and not you.
And for this feature to work, you need to make sure
you set up an S3 bucket policy
that obligates S3 Requester Pays to work.
And so the users have to be authenticated with IM
before they are able to request a data from your bucket.
But now there's a trick, right?
Because if you allow your users to access your S3 bucket
by using an assumed cross account IAM role,
then the owner of the account of that role is going
to be the one paying for the request.
So if you create a role in your account
and you give other accounts access to that role,
and then that role queries your S3 buckets,
then you're going to pay for the request
because the request comes from within your accounts.
So if you want to make sure that other accounts are paying
for the request, you do not need to use IAM role.
You need to create an S3 bucket policy
and make sure other users are authenticated using
an IAM role or IAM user that corresponds to their accounts.
And that's it.
That's all you need know about S3 cost savings.

# 135. Cloud Migration Strategies - The 7Rs
# Section: Migration
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/18376658
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's discuss
cloud migration strategies, and there is a blog on the AWS
that describe the seven Rs of cloud migration.
Now there's a very complex diagram.
We're going to go over it in time, not the diagram itself,
but the concepts behind the diagram.
What I would recommend you to do is
to actually read the blog if you can,
after this lecture, just to get a better understanding
of cloud migration,
if that's something you're interested into.
But let's go over the seven Rs
because the exam may ask you which strategy you use.
So you want to migrate to the cloud,
and the first strategy is to actually retire.
What does that mean?
That means you turn off things you don't need.
So for example, you have some services
and you actually don't need to migrate them,
so you turn them off.
It helps to also reduce the service areas for attacks
because you have more security, because you have
less services active.
You save costs because you retire services, maybe 10 to 20%,
and you focus your attention on resources
that must be maintained.
The second option is to retain.
So that means that you actually don't do a cloud migration,
which is still a decision in your cloud migration strategy.
And you may want to just retain the resource on premises,
for example, because of security, data compliance,
performance, and unresolved dependencies,
or because maybe there is no business value to migrate
or it's too complicated.
Next, we have relocate.
So relocate is actually to move your app from on-premises
to its cloud version,
or move EC2 instances to a different VPC,
a different account, or a different AWS region.
So for example, you have servers
that you manage on-premises using VMware software-defined
data centers, so SSDC, and you just want to keep the same
but use now VMware cloud on AWS,
you just relocate, but nothing has changed.
Then there is rehost for lift and shift.
So these are very simple migrations,
and what you do is that you rehost your application on AWS.
So that can be your applications,
your databases, and your data.
You're going to migrate your machines.
That could be physical, virtual, or servers
or another cloud into AWS cloud.
So here you don't do any kind of cloud optimization.
The application stays as is,
but you leverage the cloud resources.
And so possibly, by using the cloud resources,
you could save as much as 30% on cost.
And some services, for example, the
AWS application migration service,
allow you to just do that, the lift and shift.
That means you take your application
and you just put it on the cloud.
Next, we have replatform for lift and reshape.
So as an example, you want to migrate your database
into RDS, or you want to migrate your application
to Elastic Beanstalk.
So here you don't change the core architecture
of your application, but you're going
to leverage some cloud optimizations,
and you're going to save time and money
by moving to fully-managed service or a serverless service.
For example, for a database,
instead of just moving it from a server on premises to EC2,
you move it to RDS,
and RDS is going to give you a lot of benefits
around backups, around resiliency,
around high availability, and so on.
So your application hasn't changed,
but now you're using managed services.
Then we have repurchase for drop and shop.
So you move to a different product
while moving to the cloud.
For example, you want to move to a software
as a service platform, SaaS.
It's expensive in the short term, but very quick to deploy.
For example, you move your CRM
to the managed version on salesforce.com
or your HR to Workday or your CMS to Drupal.
So instead of having everything on-premises,
now you leverage SaaS platforms.
And finally, we have refactor and re-architect.
So here you want to move your application to the cloud,
but you are re-imagining how the application is going
to be architected using Cloud Native features.
So the reason you may want to do this is
because you actually want to use the cloud
to improve the scalability, the performance, security,
and agility of your application.
You may also want to break up your monolithic application
into microservices.
So this is where you're going to have the most amount
of effort, but usually the most amount of payoff
from a leveraging the cloud capabilities.
So for example, you move your application
to a serverless architecture,
or you're going to use Amazon S3
to store some data and so on.
So that's it.
I hope now the seven Rs in the cloud migration
strategy makes sense.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 136. Storage Gateway
# Section: Migration

# Caption: en_US (manual)

So AWS is starting to push for hybrid cloud,
and what is hybrid cloud?
That means that part of your infrastructure
is going to be on the cloud of AWS,
and part of your infrastructure
is going to stay on-premises,
and this can be due to multiple reasons.
Maybe you have a long cloud migration,
maybe you have security requirements
or compliance requirements, maybe it's part of your strategy
to only leverage a cloud for elastic workloads,
but to keep a lot of stuff on-premises.
So we have some services that we really like in AWS,
such as Amazon S3,
which is a proprietary storage technology,
which is unlike EFS, which is an NFS compliance file system,
so how would you expose, for example,
the S3 data on-premises?
And the bridge between this S3
and your on-premises infrastructure
is going to be AWS Storage Gateway.
So if we look at the storage cloud-native options on AWS,
we have block storage, which is Amazon EBS,
or the EC2 instance store.
We have file systems, such as Amazon EFS or Amazon FSX,
and we have object-level storage,
such as Amazon S3 or Amazon Glacier.
So now, let's talk about the AWS Storage Gateway.
So very simply, it is a bridge between your on-premises data
and your cloud data, so you have data on-premises,
and you're going to bridge it using the Storage Gateway
to the cloud.
Now, that looks simple,
but we have different use cases for this.
The first one is to do disaster recovery,
so to back up your on-premise data into the cloud,
or you can also do backup and restore,
so to do a cloud migration or to extend your storage
from on-premises to the cloud, and for example,
your cloud has colder data,
and your on-premises data has more warmer,
more frequently used data.
Also, you can, for example, instead prefer
to have the majority of your data stored on AWS
and use the Storage Gateway as an on-premises cache
for low-latency file access.
So there are different kind of use cases,
and therefore, there are different kinds of Storage Gateway,
and there are a few of them,
so the first one is the S3 File Gateway,
the Volume Gateway, and the Tape Gateway.
I will be explaining all of those in this lecture.
So first, we have the Amazon S3 File Gateway.
So we have an S3 bucket,
and we can use whatever storage class we want,
for example, S3 Standard, S3 Standard-IA, S3 One Zone-IA,
or S3 Intelligent-Tiering, but not Glacier,
and we want to connect this S3 bucket
to an on-premises application server,
but we want to use a standard network file system.
So for this, we're going to create an S3 File Gateway,
which is going to allow our application server
to use the NFS or the SMB protocol,
and by using these protocols, behind the scene,
the S3 File Gateway is going to translate those requests
into HTTPS requests for your Amazon S3 buckets.
So from an application server perspective,
it looks like it's accessing a normal file share,
but in fact, behind the scenes,
it is using an Amazon S3 buckets,
and this is how you expose S3 objects
onto on-premises application servers.
Then if you wanted to archive some of these objects,
you could create a lifecycle policy for your S3 bucket
to transition objects after a while to S3 Glacier
in order to have them archived.
So whatever buckets you configure with your S3 File Gateway
are going to be accessible using the NFS and SMB protocol,
and on top of it, the most recently used data
is cached in the File Gateway for rapid access,
so not your entire S3 bucket is on the File Gateway,
but your most recently files
that are most recently used files.
So as I said, it supports different storage classes
for your S3 buckets,
and you can transition to S3 Glacier
using a lifecycle policy.
Now, to access your bucket, you need to create IAM roles
for each File Gateway,
and then if you were to use the SMB protocol,
because it is more native for Windows file systems,
you have integration with Active Directory
for user authentication,
so that means that your users can be authentified
with your S3 File Gateway before accessing it,
and then therefore accessing your S3 buckets.
So that's the Amazon S3 File Gateway.
Next. we have the Volume Gateway,
and this is block storage using the iSCSI protocol
backed by Amazon S3,
and the idea is that you will have your volumes
being backed up by EBS snapshots,
which can, in turn, help you restore on-premises volumes
in case you need to.
So you have two types of Volume Gateway.
You have the cached volumes to get low-latency access
to the most recent volume data,
or stored volume, where the entire dataset is on-premises,
and there is a scheduled backup to Amazon S3.
So here, our application server needs to be backed up,
and so using this protocol,
we're going to get a Volume Gateway,
and the Volume Gateway will create Amazon EBS snapshots
backed by Amazon S3.
So the same logic here,
but here, the goal of the Volume Gateway really
is to back up your volumes of your on on-premises servers.
Tape Gateway is that if you have some companies that have,
for example, a tape backup system using physical tapes,
then with the Tape Gateway, you do the same process,
but the tapes are going to be backed up in the cloud,
and so this virtual tape library, or VTL,
is going to be backed by Amazon S3 and Glacier.
You're going to back up existing data
using tape-based process and using the iSCSI interface,
and then this is going to work
with leading backup software vendors.
So diagram you can expect,
the corporate data center has a backup server,
which is tape-based.
The Tape Gateway will do the interface into the cloud
by storing the tapes into Amazon S3 or in Amazon Glacier.
Finally, as you can see in all these diagrams from before,
the gateway has to be installed
on your corporate data center.
It has to run within your corporate data center,
but sometimes, you do not have virtual servers
to run this additional gateway.
So let's try to summarize the Storage Gateway service.
So we have on-premises,
where we deploy a Storage Gateway VM,
and then we have the Storage Gateway service,
and then we have the cloud of AWS.
So if we want to have a File Gateway with a local cache,
this is the use case, where we have a user group file share,
and we want to access it over the NFS or the SMB protocol.
Option number one, we connect this
into directly an S3 File Gateway,
so therefore, your data is going to be backed by Amazon S3,
and that includes many storage tiers
except Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive.
but we can create a lifecycle policy
to send this into any storage class on Amazon S3,
including S3 Glacier.
Now, the other use case for a Volume Gateway
is to have application servers mount volumes
over the iSCSI protocol.
So what we do is that this Volume Gateway
is going to be linked through Storage Gateway to Amazon S3,
so this is where the data of your volume is going to be,
and then Amazon S3 data can be transformed
into AWS EBS volumes for really being restored on AWS.
Next, we have your backup applications,
connecting over the iSCSI VTL protocol to a Tape Gateway,
and the Tape Gateway is connected to Amazon S3
as a tape library, and then we can transition these tapes
into the Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive tier
to create an archive of your tapes.
So hopefully, that summarizes everything we've seen

and then Lambda functions,

and I hope you see them.
Next we could have read only replicas.

and your applications would write some files into it.

And in another on-premise data center,

Next, there's way to do backup and lifecycle policies.

are talking to our file system on the File Gateway

we've made sure that we are getting some cost savings

So yet another thing to think about.
But this is Amazon S3,
so we have so many other possibilities.
The first one is that if you do enable
Amazon S3 ObjectVersioning,
then you can store multiple object versions
as they are modified, which is extremely helpful
if one of your engineers, or one of your employees,
is asking you to restore a specific file
to a previous version.
Because you're storing every single change in Amazon S3,
it is definitely possible for you to restore any file
to any previous version, or you can even restore
an entire file system to a previous version.
But if you do so, to restore a file
or a file system to a previous version,
you need to let your File Gateway appliance know
that there has been a change.
And so there is a cache, a RefreshCache API
on the gateway so that you notify the gateway
that there has been some restore happening,
some changes happening on the Amazon S3 buckets,
and there will be a synchronization happening
in the backend.
Another one is to use Amazon S3 Object Lock.
And this enables the File Gateway
to be a Write Once Read Many,
so WORM data network file system.
So the idea is that if there are any modifications
or renames in the file share clients,
the file gateway will create a new version
of the object without affecting prior versions
and the original locked version will remain unchanged.
Effectively, the giving, making sure
that you're not losing any data
and that the original data will never be deleted.

the Amazon S3 Adapter for Snowball,
which has a data transfer rate
of typically 250 megabytes per second

# 140. AWS DMS - Database Migration Services
# Section: Migration
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/18376666
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk about DMS,
which is a Database Migration Service.
This allows you, as the name indicates,
to quickly and securely migrate databases to AWS.
The beautiful thing is that it's resilient and self-healing,
so your database migration job can recover from failure.
The source database will remain available
during the migration, which is a good thing.
That means you can keep on using the source database
while migrating to the target database
and then safely migrate your application over.
It supports many different things.
It supports homogenous migrations.
For example, if you migrate an Oracle database
to another Oracle database.
It supports heterogeneous migration,
which is when you have a different database engine.
For example, for Microsoft SQL Server to Aurora.
And also it supports Continuous Data Replication using CDC
so that you can do one of migrations
or continuous migrations using CDC.
And for this, you need to create an EC2 instance
that will perform the replication tasks for you.
So the idea is very simple.
The source database is on-premise.
We're going to create an EC2 instance
that will be running the DMS software,
and then it will insert the data into the target database.
Now what are the sources for DMS as well as the targets?
Well, for sources, we have on-premises
and EC2 instance databases such as Oracle,
Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, MariaDB,
PostgreSQL, MongoDB, SAP, and DB2.
So a wide variety of databases.
Azure, so any Azure SQL Database.
Also, you can migrate
all Amazon RDS databases, including Aurora.
Amazon S3, and then MongoDB's running on DocumentDB.
Now for targets of DMS, we have any on-premises
and EC2 instances database such as Oracle,
Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, and SAP.
But also Amazon RDS, including Aurora, Amazon Redshift,
Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, the OpenSearch Service,
the Kinesis Data Streams, and DocumentDB.
So a few things to note is that Amazon Redshift,
and Kinesis Date Streams, and OpenSearch Service
are not sources, they are targets of DMS.
So hopefully, that helps you for your exam.
So AWS SCT, for Schema Conversion Tool,
which is to convert your database schema
from one engine to another.
For example, if you're doing an OLTP, for example,
from SQL Server or Oracle into MySQL, PostgreSQL, or Aurora,
then you have to change the database engine.
And, so, you're going to use SCT.
For OLAP, for example, you want to migrate
from Teradata or Oracle into Redshift.
So here's the example.
In this example, SCT will be running alongside DMS
to convert the schema from the source database
to the targets.
The one thing you have to remember is that you do not need
to use SCT if you are migrating the same database engine.
For example, if you're doing on-premise PostgreSQL
to RDS PostgreSQL, this is the same DB engine.
This is still PostgreSQL, and RDS is the platform.
And if you remember, this migration
from on-premise PostgreSQL to RDS PostgreSQL
is called a re-platform type of migration.
Okay, some good things to know about DMS.
First of all, it works over VPC Peering
if you wanted to move from one VPC to another.
It works over VPN, either site to site or software,
or it works for Direct Connect.
It supports three kinds of load.
Full Load, which is a one-time full load extract and load.
Full Load + CDC.
So you have some continuous data replication
after the first initial load.
Or CDC only to just stream changes.
For Oracle, it supports TDE for the source
using something called a BinaryReader.
And for the target, it supports
Binary Large Objects, so BLOBs,
in tables that will have a primary key,
and it also supports TDE.
So the idea here is that if you are migrating a BLOB data
into an RDS Oracle, then you need to make sure
that there is a primary key associated alongside that BLOB.
For OpenSearch, as I said, the source does not exist,
and for the target, it's possible to migrate
from a relational database to OpenSearch using DMS.
So that means that DMS cannot be used
to replicate OpenSearch data.
You cannot have OpenSearch as a source
and so, therefore, if you wanted to replicate
OpenSearch data somewhere else,
you would need to get some tools specific to OpenSearch,
maybe to export it into Amazon S3,
and then being able to send it wherever you want.
But DMS is only used to have the target being OpenSearch.
So that means, for example,
you can have MySQL migrated into OpenSearch through DMS.
Finally, and very important going into the exam,
you can combine Snowball and DMS.
So in case you're doing a very large database migration,
you may have terabytes and terabytes
of the information or data.
And, so, in case you wanted to go
everything over the network, that may not be possible.
Maybe because your network bandwidth is too little,
or maybe because you have way too much data.
And we've seen, from before, that Snowball is a great way
to migrate data, large amount of it, into AWS.
So you can combine Snowball and DMS together to do so.
So how does that work?
The following stages happen.
First, you're going to use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool,
SCT, to extract the data locally,
so we're talking about on-premise,
and then we'll copy it onto a Snowball Edge device.
Then you're shipping the Snowball Edge device back to AWS.
And then after AWS receives your shipment,
the Edge device will automatically load its data
onto the Amazon S3 bucket, and then DMS will kick in.
It will take the files from the S3 bucket,
migrate the data into the target store,
and then if you're using CDC on top of it,
any updates that have happened while your Snowball device
is being shipped, will be replicated afterwards
to the target data store.
And here, we get a really good advantage.
We get the speed and the efficiency of Snowball
and the continuous data replication out of DMS.
So using Snowball and DMS is a great combo and, again,
something you have to remember going into the exam.
So that's it for it.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

Now let's talk

because you're actually creating chaos
within your infrastructure.
So why do we do this?
Well to make sure our application is really solid,
and this allows us to uncover hidden bugs
and performance bottlenecks.
And currently, FIS supports some services,
you don't need to know them all,
so here's a list and maybe there'll be others over time,

ECS by stopping ECS tasks, EKS, and so on
to stop a Kubernetes task and RDS to make failures
go alongside our database.
So how does that work?
Well, we have FIS and we're going to create experiments.

to generate these disruptions,
and then they're going to have disruptions on resources.
So really you have to choose what happens
to your EC2 instances, what happens to your ECS clusters,

# 152. PrivateLink
# Section: VPC

# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk about AWS PrivateLink,
which is also called VPC Endpoint Services.
So PrivateLink is going to be the most secure
and scalable way to expose the service to thousands of VPC,
either your own VPC or other accounts.
Why?
Because you can expose a service within your own VPC
privately to others without doing any sort of VPC peering,
using an internet gateway, NAT gateways
or NAT instances, and route tables.
So the idea is that we still allow other people
to access our application,
but very securely by really protecting our network
to just one PrivateLink.
So here's an example.
We are the service VPC and we have created an application
and it's an application service,
and we want to be able to give access
to other customers in other accounts access
to our application.
So here is a customer VPC,
and they will have consumer applications,
and they want to be able to connect
to our application service.
We could obviously do a VPC peering and that would work,
but the problem of VPC peering would be
that all the customer VPC instances would be able to talk
to all the instances in my VPC,
and that makes me way too exposed
from a network perspective.
I could also go over the public internet,
but this is not really good
because then that means that my service needs
to be publicly accessible, and I don't like that.
So what I really want is to be able to go
through a PrivateLink.
So for this, I have to create a network load balancer
in my service VPC
and in the Elastic Network Interface and my customer VPC.
So now my application is going to be exposed through an NLB,
and on the customer VP side,
there will be an ENI being created.
And then the magic happens.
There's going to be AWS PrivateLink.
And with PrivateLink, there's going
to be a private connection between the ENI
and the network load balancer.
And so for our customer VPC,
to access our application service, they just need
to talk to the ENI.
The ENI will forward the traffic
onto the network load balancer,
and the network load balancer will forward traffic
onto the application service.
And here we go, we have a PrivateLink.
And this is hugely scalable
because we can do this a thousand times.
We just need one network load balancer
and as many ENI as target customer VPC that we have.
So if the NLB is going to be in multiple availability zone,
then you need to make sure your ENI are also going
to be in multiple AZ and then we have a solution
that is going to be fault tolerance.
So I found PrivateLink
to be revolutionary to work really great.
It's really scalable, and you have to remember it going
into the exam.
So let's consider how to make PrivateLink works
for Amazon S3 with Direct Connects.
So here's the issue.
We have a corporate data center
and want to access our Amazon S3 bucket
through Direct Connect connection.
And we have two options, right?
Number one is to use a public VIF so that the traffic goes
from direct connect to the public URL
of Amazon S3, but through Direct Connect.
The other option if we wanted to make all traffic go
through your VPC would be to create a VPC endpoint.
Now you cannot use a gateway endpoint in this case
because gateway endpoints only works from within your VPC.
So if your EC2 instances wanted to connect
to Amazon S3, fine, use a gateway endpoint.
But the corporate data center
through Direct Connect cannot access the gateway endpoint.
Therefore, we have to create an interface VPC endpoint
for Amazon S3 that is linked to a PrivateLink.
And therefore, for Direct Connect
to access your PrivateLink,
you must create a private VIF,
which then allows you to keep all traffic private
through your VPC into your Amazon S3 bucket.
Another architecture you must know is how
to use PrivateLink VPC endpoints cross region.
So here's the idea.
You want to access an S3 bucket in eu-west-1,
you have EC2 instances as a service in ap-east-1
and you want to access those from us-east-1.
So the previous solution was requiring VPC peering,
but now if you use PrivateLink, you don't even need it.
So how to do this?
Well, you create a VPC interface endpoint
for Amazon S3 directly in your us-east-1 VPC,
and you can link it to a service in another region,
which gives you private connectivity

Also, if you expose your EC2 instances

Because now we can do VPC peering

VPC B as well cannot access your corporate data center.

of celebrities to find people in your images as well.
So the use cases for Rekognition is to take your image
and do labeling images and video
and to labeling, content moderation, text detection,
face detection and analysis,
for example, find the gender, the age range
and the emotions that are associated with these faces,
do a face search and verification,
do celebrity recognition,
as well as pathing.
So for example, if you're doing a sports game analysis
of a video, so that's a high level.
Remember Rekognition is about images and videos.
So on the Rekognition website
we can see we can automate our image and video analysis
with machine learning.
And I really like this website
because it shows you how it works.
So for example,
for this image we can identify the elements of this image.
For example, a person, a rock, a mountain bike,
a crest and outdoors.
We can label, for example, what we see in images,
for example, golden retrievers or dogs.
Then I can look at content moderation
to make sure that it's appropriate for all ages.
I can detect text, for example, for a run.
We want to see the numbers of each runner in the run.
We can do face detection analysis,
for example, this person looks happy.
She's smiling,
her eyes are open and she's a female.
Face search and verification,
maybe if you have a security application.
Finally, if you want to recognize a celebrity,
you can take a picture of them.
And this is the CTO of AWS.
And then finally, pathing,
for example, if you're monitoring a soccer game,
you could see where everyone is going to do
maybe some real time analytics.
And there's one feature you need to know about
going into the exam.
It's around content moderation.
So this is used to detect content that is inappropriate,
unwanted, or offensive in images and videos.
So this will be used, for example,
if you have a social network or if you broadcast media
or if you do advertising or if you're doing e-commerce
and you need to create a safe user experience
and make sure the image is displayed,
don't show any kind of content that would be
deemed offensive by some people.
For example, racist content
or pornography or other kind of things like this.
So how does that work?
Well, the image will be analyzed by Amazon Rekognition
and then you set a Minimum Confidence Threshold
for items that will be flagged.
So you set it to whatever percentage you want.
And obviously the lower you set this percentage
the more matches you're going to get.
And this confidence percentage represents how
confident Amazon Rekognition is
that this flagged image represents indeed
some inappropriate or offensive character.
And then once you have done this
and you flagged some images,
you may want to do a human manual review.
And so to do so,
you can use something called Amazon Augmented AI
called A2I
and you do optional manual review
directly in Amazon A2I.
And all of this process right here allows you to
automatically flag images that can be sensitive
and then use a final manual review
to know whether or not you want to keep them or delete them.
And this can help you with comply
with regulations in case you must detect
these kind of content
before they're posted to your applications.

So, Comprehend is really about getting a lot of data in
and then Comprehend will do the rest
to try to understand the meaning of that data.

and structuring it around these features.

or NLP, are for example, to analyze customer interaction.
So say you have a bunch of customers sending you emails
and you want to understand overall based
on your support service what leads to a positive
or negative experience from your customers.
So we use Comprehend to extract these features
and then you will have the business insight

You can also, for example, create

So imagine you have a lot of articles

# 173. CICD
# Section: Other Services
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/18376692
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk about CICD.
CICD is a bigger focus in the certified developer exam
but you still need to know how it works
from a solution architecture perspective.
So, let's go back to the basics.
Continuous integration helps
because developers push the code very often
to a code repository
and that could be GitHub, CodeCommit, or Bitbucket.
So the developers push the code,
and what you need to do is make sure that
the code that they push is valid and can be built.
So, you would have a build or a test server
that will check the code as soon as it's pushed.
And services that help with this
is CodeBuild on AWS for example,
or Jenkins CI or other ones.
And so the idea is that
the build server will retrieve the code
from the code repository,
build it and test it to see if it validates
what it needs to be done.
Then the developers will get feedback about the test
and checks that have passed or failed.
And so in case there's a failure,
the good thing is that we are getting bugs early
and we can fix them as soon as possible.
So continuous integration now
is into every modern company's workflow.
And the idea is that
you are going to deliver your software faster
because the code is tested continuously.
And finally, thanks to this,
we are going to deploy more often
and the developers are happier
because they don't need to run the test
on their own machine,
they can wait for the build server to run the test for them
and sometimes test suites can take long time to run.
And then we have continuous delivery.
Continuous delivery is to ensure
that the software can be released reliably whenever needed.
So the idea is that we are going to deploy often
and it needs to be a quick deployment.
So we want to shift away
from that mindset of one release every three months,
that can be catastrophic.
Two, let's do five releases a day
and then every release is very safe.
That usually means that we have to automate
the way we deploy our application
onto our infrastructure.
And some services that can help with this
is going to be AWS CodeDeploy
or Jenkins Continuous Delivery or Spinnaker or some others.
So let's look at what it looks like.
The developers push the code often
and we have the continuous integration part
that gets to code, build it and test it.
And then once the build has passed,
there will be a deployment server that will be deploying
the application every single time the build passes.
And so our application is going to be in version one
and the deployment after it happens will go to version two.
And as we go and push more code,
we're gonna get more and more deployments.
So, there's the technology stack for CICD in AWS.
There is the phase of code, build, test, deploy
and then provision the infrastructure to deploy on.
So, CodeCommit is a code repository
and this is the AWS version.
The similar service offered online is GitHub
or you can use a third party code repository
but this is not in an AWS native.
Then once the code is in CodeCommit
you're going to have to build it and test it.
And for this you use AWS CodeBuild
and this is a great service for doing both these things.
And the beautiful thing is that there's no time limit
to however long your builds can run.
So it is better than using say Lambda functions
to test your code.
So CodeBuild is the way to go
when you want to build and test your code on AWS.
But a similar alternative is going to be
a bit more open source
and cross cloud providers
is going to be something like Jenkins CI
or a third party CI server.
And then for deploying and provisioning,
we have multiple options.
Beanstalk works really well
because we can provision the infrastructure with Beanstalk
and also use Beanstalk to deploy our application gradually
to our EC2 instances.
Or we could use a EC2 fleet that we manage ourselves.
Maybe we have created it using CloudFormation
and then we would use something
like CodeDeploy to deploy our code
to this EC2 instance fleet.
And how do we manage the orchestration
of all these steps in our CICD?
Well, for this, we're going to use AWS CodePipeline
which is allowing us to define a pipeline
to orchestrate all the steps.
So, let's do through a real example
of how CICD architecture looks like in a company
and this is something you're expected to know
and this is going to be the extent
of what you're going to be texted on
at the exam from a SA Pro perspective.
So, the code is going to be in CodeCommit
and you're going to have different branches for your code,
the dev branch and the prod branch.
A branch is basically a version of the code
that's going to be independent from another branch.
And so while you do development,
you're going to be modifying the development branch.
And then when you'll be done,
you're going to merge the changes
from the development branch into the production branch.
So, what happens with the development branch
then we're going to define a development code pipeline
and what it will do inside
is build the code using CodeBuild,
maybe test it as well
and the CodeBuild is going to source the code
from the developer branch of CodeCommits.
Then once it's built and tested,
we're going to deploy often,
so we'll hook it up to CodeDeploy through CodePipeline
and then CodeDeploy may deploy us, for example
to a Beanstalk environment in depth,
or it could be an ASG or something different.
So it's really up to you to see how you wanna do it.
Then the dev branch will get merged into the prod branch
once we're ready to be in a good state for application.
So, the way we do it is that
we look at the Elastic Beanstalk dev environment
and say, yes, the Elastic Beanstalk environment
does look good,
I'm happy with the state of my application,
I want to release it to all my users globally,
therefore, I'm going to take the code from my dev branch,
do a pull request and merge it into the prod branch.
So we're going to create a prod code pipeline
and we're going to do a CodeBuild
to build that prod branch,
a CodeDeploy to deploy the changes into say
a production environment for Elastic Beanstalk.
But again, you have different options.
It could be CloudFormation,
all these kind of things, okay?
And this is the idea of CICD architecture.
So, what you need to get out of this is that
you need to create one CodePipeline per branch
in your CodeCommit repository.
There is no way of doing one CodePipeline for both.
And then each pipeline itself will have its own instance
of CodeBuild, CodeDeploy
and its own Elastic Beanstalk environment
to properly separate
your dev and your prod environments.
Another important architecture
is around using Lambda with CodeCommits.
So, when you push code into CodeCommits
every commit can trigger a Lambda function.
And this Lambda function can do a lot of things,
but for example it can scan for leaked AWS credentials
on every code push
and disable them automatically to remedy the issue.
So, how does that work?
Well, the developer pushes code into CodeCommits,
CodeCommit invokes Lambda function
and the Lambda function has some special code
to scan for credentials.
If they are found,
then the Lambda function can do an API call
to disable access keys in IAM
and also lock the CodeCommit repository
and also send a notification into an SNS topic
that would be directly linked
to notify an administrator by email, for example.
Other good things to know about CICD is that
you can use a manual approval stage in CodePipeline.
You can run unit tests using CodeCommit,
CodeBuild, and CodePipeline.
So, how?
So you create a CodePipeline
you push code into CodeCommit which is your source
and then on every push
then your tests are going to be running within CodeBuild.
You can also build and store Docker images automatically
using CodeBuild an ECR.
So how?
Well, whenever you are building an image,
then the script within CodeBuild
is going to build a Docker image
and then push it into Amazon ECR using some commands.
And then finally,
you can do automated CloudFormation deployment
using CodePipeline by first pushing it,
for example, to a CodeCommit,
and then using the CodePipeline deploy stage
to deploy your CloudFormation templates.
You also need to know how CodePipeline
and GitHub have integrations.
So, there are two versions of this integration.
The first one is the version one
and you have GitHub and CodePipeline.
And one option within the version one
is to make sure that CodePipeline regularly checks
your GitHub repository for changes.
So it will happen every X number of minutes
or X number of seconds,
and that's not very efficient.
The other more efficient way
is to have GitHub actually set up in the HTTP webhook
so that they can send notifications to CodePipeline
whenever the repository is actually updated.
So this is for version one
but now there's also a new version
of this integration called version two
in which GitHub and CodePipeline are linked
through what's called a CodeStar Source Connection.
The CodeStar Source Connection
is actually a GitHub application,
and then through this connection automatically
any changes pushed to GitHub
will be picked up by CodePipeline.
So, that's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 176. AWS WorkSpaces
# Section: Other Services
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/18376710
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So workspaces is going to give you a
managed secure Cloud desktop.
This is a great way to eliminate management
of on-premise VDI.
And VDI means virtual desktop infrastructure.
The idea with workspaces is that,
for example you want to get access to
Windows machine on the cloud
and you want to get into it,
then you would use workspaces to create
that virtual desktop.
That is going to be a Windows
and then you will get into that Windows,
and you can operate your desktop from there.
You can even pay per hour, which is on demand pricing
or have a monthly subscription for unlimited usage.
It's going to be secure, encrypted
and get Network isolation.
It is integrated with Microsoft Active Directory
so all your machines can join your directory domain
if you needed to.
The user are going to get into a virtual desktop
and that could be Linux or Windows.
And then securely,
this virtual desktop can access, for example
your corporate data center or can access your virtual cloud.
So there's a good way, for example,
to give you reserves access to an environment you trust,
where you know the network security is going to be optimal.
Now, workspaces has something called
Workspaces Application Manager or WAM
and this is important you know.
So this is to deploy and manage applications
as visualized application containers.
The idea is that you're going to containerize
this application
and deploy them onto all your workspaces.
You can provision them at scale,
and you keep the application updated using WAM.
This is different from Windows updates.
So Workspaces Applications manager is just for applications
whereas Windows updates is going to be
well for the updates of your Windows machine.
So by default, Amazon workspaces are configured
to install software updates and by default,
any workspace that you create that has Windows installed,
will also have Windows update turned on.
And then you have full control over how often
you want Windows update to run,
but it runs during maintenance windows.
So during this maintenance windows,
the updates are going to be installed
and you define the maintenance window that you want.
So you have always on workspaces, and by default
the maintenance window is going to be between midnight
and 4:00 AM on Sunday morning,
or we get auto stop workspaces,
which are the workspaces that stop
when the users don't use them.
And in this case, the users don't use them often enough,
then these workspaces are automatically started once a month
to install the windows updates,
whereas for always on,
well, because the workspaces always on
this is for sure going to happen between midnight
and 4:00 AM on Sunday mornings.
Finally, you can also define a manual maintenance window
and you define your windows,
the instances of workspace will be offline for a moment
for your users,
and you can perform the maintenance you want
on these workspaces.
Next we have cross region redirection for Amazon workspaces.
So the idea is that we want to run workspaces directories
in multiple regions.
So we have a primary region and then we have
a failover region.
So the idea is that
when the users connect into the primary region,
the workspace directory is going to be connected,
for example, to AWS Managed Microsoft AD
to store these users
and allow them to open sessions on workspaces.
And if you want to have a failover region,
what you need to create is you need to create
an AD connector in that failover region.
So why an AD connector
and not a multi-region managed Microsoft AD?
Well, the documentation says that right now
the multi-region manage Microsoft AD is not supported.
So you have to use an AD connector.
So now we have two regions
and we need to set up connection aliases.
So you sub condition aliases
and then you create a record in Route 53.
And this record is for desktop.example.com,
and it's a text kind of record with type failover.
So the idea now is that
your workspace is going to have a connection alias
in the primary region and a connection alias
in the secondary region, the failover region.
And we point both of them into
the Route 53 text record for deskstop.example.com.
And that means that if the primary region is up,
then when users enter the desktop.example.com to connect
to workspaces, the text record is going to be corresponding
to the one of the region that is primary,
and then if we set up a health check and an alarm
to failover to the secondary region,
then in case we have failover,
then Route 53 will respond to desktop.example.com
for a text record,
to the region code of the failover region.
Therefore, our users can correctly connect
to the primary region and in case
connect to the secondary region.
Now, when they connect to one region or the other one,
the user data is not persistent
because the user data is region specific
and the workspaces are region specific.
And so therefore, if you wanted to have data being shared
between the two regions that the users actually don't see
that they're being failed over to another region
then you can use, for example, Amazon workDocs,
which is going to give you persistence for the user data.
Another thing you need to know for Amazon workspaces
is IP access control groups
which is very simple.
It's basically security groups for Amazon workspaces.
So it's a list of IP addresses and CIDR address ranges
that users are authorized to connect from.
So for example, if you have a corporate data center
and you have a user
and has a public IP from a CIDR that's owned
by the data center from a public CIDR,
then you can set up an IP access control group
to make sure that only this CIDR is allowed to access your
workspace directory,
and therefore your users to use workspaces.
So it's an extra security, just like security groups.
In case your users are accessing workspaces
through a VPN or a NAT.
Then of course the IP access control group
must allow the public IP of the VPN or the NAT connection.
Okay, so that's it for workspaces,
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

specific AWS APIs, or the SMTP protocol.

# 181. Amazon Pinpoint
# Section: Other Services
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/42360086
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's talk about Amazon Pinpoint.
And Amazon Pinpoint is scalable two ways,
so inbound and outbound marketing communication service.
The idea is that you want to send email,
SMS, push notifications, voice,
and in-app messaging through Pinpoint.
And one of the main use cases is SMS.
So the customers will receive an SMS
that you send from Amazon Pinpoint.
And you have the ability to segment
and personalize the messages
with the right content to customers.
So you can create groups and segments and so on.
You also have the possibility to,
of course, receive replies.
And this scales to billions of messages per day.
So the use cases for Pinpoint is to run campaigns
by sending marketing email in bulk,
or sending transactional SMS messages.
And should someone reply or should it be successful,
then all the events such as text success,
text delivered replies, and so on,
will be delivered to Amazon SNS,
Kinesis Data Firehose, and CloudWatch Logs.
So you can build any kind of automation
easily on top of Amazon Pinpoint.
And so you may be wondering,
well, what is the difference between Pinpoint
and Amazon SNS or Amazon SES?
Because there is obviously some overlap.
So the idea is that in SNS or SES,
you have to manage each message's audience,
content, and delivery schedule.
And this is the responsibility of your application.
And that may be a lot of work,
and that may be not very scalable.
So in Amazon Pinpoint, instead, you're going to create
message templates, delivery schedules,
highly targeted segments, and full campaigns.
And all of this is managed by the Pinpoint service.
So see Pinpoint as the next evolution of SNS and SES,
in case you wanna do full-blown
marketing communications service.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 182. EC2 Image Builder
# Section: Other Services
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/34782972
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
the EC2 Image Builder service.
So it's a service used to create and automate the creation
of virtual machines or container images.
So basically you want to automate the creation,
maintain, and validate and test your EC2 AMIs.
So you can run the Image Builder on a schedule.
For example, build an AMI every week
or whenever packages are updated, et cetera, et cetera.
Or you can run it
with some automation as we'll see in the next slide.
It's a free service
so you only pay for the underlying resources created
and these are EC2 instances
as I will show you right now.
On top of it, once you create an AMI
from the EC2 Image Builder service,
you can publish that AMI to multiple regions
and multiple accounts.
Which is going to help with your distribution.
So the EC2 Image Builder service, once you set it up
and you set up, you build instructions,
is going to create a builder EC2 instance.
It's an instance that comes with almost nothing on it.
And then the Image Builder service is going to
run what's called the Build Components to
customize the software on your instance,
based on the instructions you gave it.
So it's going to build your AMI as it goes.
Then when the build instructions are done,
the AMI is going to be created from it,
and this AMI is going to be tested.
So a new EC2 instance,
from that AMI is going to be created.
All the tests are going to be run on the AMI,
for example to test if the AMI is working,
if it's secure and so on.
And then the image, the image itself,
so the AMI, is going to be distributed,
of course in the region it was created,
but also to other regions if you wanted to,
and to multiple accounts if you need to.
Which really gives you a central way
to build your AMIs on AWS.
So let's have a look at the CICD architecture
for the EC2 Image Builder service.
So first we have a CodePipeline to orchestrate everything,
and within the CodePipeline we start
from CodeCommit to get our code source.
So we're going to create our application there
and then it's going to be passed onto CodeBuild so that
the application is being built, the code is being compiled,
and then we have an executable.
Then once the application is ready to be shipped,
we need to build an AMI,
and therefore we're going to use CloudFormation.
Which is going to automate
and launch the EC2 Image Builder service,
which is going to take the code,
lastly built from CodeBuild
and then create an AMI out of it.
So this is the stage two, where we build this AMI
and the stage three is the rollout of this AMI.
So again, we're going to use a CloudFormation template,
this time to perform a rolling update
onto an auto scaling group,
where EC2 instances are using the previous AMI,
and therefore CloudFormation has some logic to
upgrade your images once at a time.
So your instances are going to be upgraded
over time from the old AMI to the new AMI,
and that gives you a fully automated way to push code
into CodeCommit to build an AMI from it,
and to roll out the AMI in production to your instances.
So that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 183. AWS IoT Core
# Section: Other Services
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-solutions-architect-professional/learn/lecture/34783296
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about the AWS IoT Core service.
So IoT, if you don't know, stands for Internet of Things.
It's the network of all these internet-connected devices
that are able to collect and transfer data.
So thanks to the IoT Core service,
you can easily connect devices to the cloud.
For example, if you have IoT devices onto smart cars,
then you can very easily connect them to the cloud.
That means that you can have a serverless secure
and scalable solution,
so you can have billions of devices
and trillions of messages.
And through the IoT Core service,
they're going to be published and subscribed for messages
so they can communicate with one another
or your applications.
On top of it, IoT Core has integrations
with many AWS services such as Lambda,
S3, SageMaker, and so on.
And thanks to this,
you can build your IoT applications to gather,
process, analyze, and act on this data rapidly.
So while you don't need to be an expert
in the IoT Core service,
it's important to know the integrations.
So IoT Topics are topics just like SNS Topics,
they take data in.
And so the kind of data it takes in, for example,
could be using the MQTT protocol.
So it receives an MQTT message,
then you set up IoT rules for these messages
and the rules have actions
and these actions can be related to AWS services.
For example, these messages from your IoT Topic
can be sent to Kinesis, DynamoDB, SQS,
MSK, SNS, S3, Lambda, and so on.
So one of these integrations you need to know more
is the Kinesis Data Firehose integration,
but it's very easy to understand.
Again, your IoT Core receives MQTT messages
and they can be sent near real time
into an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
where you can operate some transformations on these messages
using a Lambda function
and then persist these messages into Amazon S3,
Redshift, and Amazon OpenSearch, for example.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture, very short,
but hopefully you get the idea behind IoT Core.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

from the Lambda function.

and fails three times after doing three retries
because it's been invoked asynchronously,
then the message will be lost and will not be invoked.

is that if somehow something goes wrong,

Number two is that every EC2 instance
is going to invoke Lambda functions

into an SQS queue.

D is to adjust the concurrency limit
